speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to table a copy of order in council P.C. 3456, passed on the 14th day of August, rescinding the regulations respecting the distribution of motor vehicles.
As the house will recall, during the period from May 7 to June 30 applications for priority certificates were accepted and processed but, due to the number of certificates outstanding and not honoured, the issue of the certificates was suspended until July 1, when all which had been approved during this period were issued. After the 1st July no applications were accepted, except in very special circumstances. On August 1 the controller's orders were amended to prohibit the sale or delivery by a dealer of a new passenger car or truck to anyone who was not the holder of a priority certificate. Since then new passenger cars and trucks have been delivered only to holders of a priority certificate. It is now felt that the distribution of motor vehicles can best be handled by normal trade channels, and the regulations have accordingly been rescinded.
I should remind the house that price ceilings on motor vehicles are fixed by the wartime prices and trade board, and that the rescinding of these regulations does not remove or affect the price ceilings on motor vehicles.

speakeroldname: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW METHOD OF DEALING WITH ABSENTEES AND DESERTERS
speechtext:
I desire to announce that a new method has been adopted of dealing

Armed Forces-Absentees
with absentees and deserters from the armed
forces. The new method will apply to all service personnel who went absent on or before 1st January, 1946, and who had not been apprehended or had not surrendered themselves before 15th August, 1946. It will not apply to those who deserted or went absent while serving overseas. The order in council authorizing the new method, provides that such persons shall be deemed never to have served in the armed forces of Canada and consequently shall not be entitled to any of the rights, privileges or benefits normally accorded to members of the armed forces.
The new method to be now adopted was approved by the Prime Minister prior to his departure for the Paris peace conference. The order in council authorizing the new method of dealing with absentees and deserters was passed yesterday and the effective date fixed as to-day, August 15.
At the present time there are approximately 14,000 army absentees and deserters still unapprehended of whom approximately 8,200 are N.R.M.A. personnel and 5,800 general service personnel; 155 in the navy and 140 in the R.C.A.F. During the war, and from the end of the war up to the present time, active efforts were made by the services to apprehend absentees and deserters. When apprehended or after surrendering they were tried by service authorities. A period of detention normally followed. This has required the maintenance at a substantial cost of special service establishments such as provost corps, staffs at headquarters and depots, and military detention barracks, to apprehend, discipline and retain in custody the absentees and deserters. Further expenditures are incurred upon the issuance of rations and quarters, medical and dental treatment, clothing and equipment, as well as dependents' allowance for the dependents of those in detention.
When such absentees and deserters have served their sentences they are discharged from the armed forces and at that time they normally receive a clothing allowance of $100, plus other rehabilitation benefits, including in many cases a war service gratuity and rehabilitation grant based on the period of satisfactory service but not including the time spent while absent without leave or in detention. In addition there are other benefits of real value for which they may be eligible, including disability pensions, assistance under the Veterans' Land Act and the like. Such personnel are entitled to dental treatment at the time of discharge as well as free medical treatment for the first year after discharge. This new method will have, therefore, the result of
imposing a penalty by the removal of benefits to which such personnel would otherwise be entitled and, at the same time, effecting substantial economies in both manpower and financial outlay.
Numerous requests and representations
have been made from time to time during the past year for a general amnesty as was granted on December 20, 1919 after the last war. The method which has been adopted imposes an automatic penalty which deprives absentees and deserters of the benefits which they might otherwise derive as members or former members of the armed forces.
The method which I have outlined applies only to those absent before January 1, 1946 and is not intended to include the casual shortterm absentee who continues as a normal problem of the three services. While length of absence is not an infallible guide as to the intention not to return to service, it is a general indication that the absentee does not voluntarily intend to return. It was thought that all absentees who merited any real consideration have had more than a fair opportunity for the past several months to come forward voluntarily.
Absentees and deserters who had been apprehended or who surrendered themselves prior to 15th August 1946 and who are at present serving sentences will have, subject to the usual provisions, the compensating advantages and benefits which I have mentioned. Under existing regulations all sentences of absentees and deserters at present in detention are reviewed regularly and remissions granted where desirable. This policy will continue with more frequent reviews being made.
Absentees and deserters who under the new procedure are, deemed never to have served will, of course, not receive any form of discharge certificate from the Canadian services.
I wish to table copy of order in council P.C. 3264 to which I have referred.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: DISCONTINUANCE AS OP AUGUST 15-REVOCATION OF MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have to inform the house that under order in council P.C. 3449 of August 14, 1946, national registration has been discontinued as from to-day August 15. It is provided by the same order in council that further prosecutions shall not be entered against anyone accused of an infraction under the national registration regulations, 1940, nor shall pending cases be proceeded with.
I should like to briefly review the salient features of the registration when now announcing its termination.
At a time when France had fallen and Great Britain was already being subjected to the most violent action the enemy could put against her, when indeed the shadow of actual invasion over this country appeared to offer some grim prospect of reality, it was agreed that existing data on Canada's human resources was inadequate for total war purposes.
Within two months of the collapse of France all plans had been laid for the national registration of civilian residents of Canada over sixteen years of age, and registration was made during August, 1940.
With the assistance of an army of volunteer registrars, forms were completed by 7,862,920 persons, of whom, 3,979.680 were males and 3,883,240 females.
Made under the National Resources Mobilization Act, the registration was taken for, and kept up to date by the Department of National War Services, until March, 1942, when it was transferred to the Department of Labour to assist toward wartime control of manpower.

Since 1940 keeping the fundamental data of the registration up to date has involved a total of about eight million changes, including new addresses, marriages, deaths, corrections, new registrations, and so forth-about the same number as there were persons registered originally.
The data yielded by the registration was used for a variety of purposes, but chiefly for the following:-
(a)	The military call-up for the army.
(b)	Procurement of skilled workers for essential industries.
(c)	Indexing of technical personnel.
(d)	Listing of doctors and nurses.
(e)	Identification of individuals for a variety of purposes.
(f)	Listing of certain foreign nationals of allied nations, available for military service under those countries.
I should like to express my sincere appreciation to the staff engaged on the registration while in the Department of Labour, and to the postmasters across the country who acted as agents, and without whose assistance the keeping up to date of the registration would have been extremely difficult.
The same order in council, P.C. 3449, revokes the national selective service mobilization regulations, 1944, as from August 15. Earlier this year the thirteen mobilization boards had been dissolved, and the thirteen registrars' offices across Canada had been closed out. The order in council provides that further action will not be instituted in the courts against any offenders under the mobilization regulations, nor will court proceedings now pending be proceeded with.
At this point I should like to explain that the action taken now follows after veiy strenuous efforts to locate all men of military call-up age who could not be found again after first registering. In addition to using the services of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and other police forces throughout Canada and checking through government contacts with the population, we have used several established tracing agencies for some years. The various methods used did, of course, succeed in locating many outstanding delinquents, but it is our opinion that the 1,563 who failed to respond to our orders, and who have not yet been traced, could hardly be located, even through further efforts.
The total of men not yet located has been reduced to 6,553-this out of a grand total of 1,859,811 men dealt with under mobilization regulations. But this number of 6,553 contains mostly men who have left the country, or who apparently are dead, or who registered more

Questions
than once under assumed names, or are in other unusual categories. The possible delinquents are represented by the figure of 1,563, to which I have referred already. Thus, at most, men not yet located, and thought to be delinquent under the regulations, represent only one-twelfth of one per cent of the grand total, 1,859,811.
Figures on the military call-up were frequently given to the house in the past, so at this time I think that in addition to the figures I have, mentioned already, it is only necessary to mention that somewhat more than 800,000 of the men dealt with under mobilization regulations are recorded as in the armed services at one time or another.
Originally, of course, the military call-up came under the Department of National War Services, but its administration had been transferred to the Department of Labour at December 1, 1942.
To the members of the judiciary and the other gentlemen who served on the mobilization boards, I wish to express my sincere appreciation once again. Their responsibilities were grave, and their duties were onerous. They had to decide between important wartime industries and the urgent need of men for the armed services. I suggest that without exception they discharged their duties in a conscientious and fair manner, and that they deserve our gratitude. Also the registrars and their staffs deserve credit for the manner in which they carried through their responsibilities.
I am happy that we have reached the day when we are able to dispense finally with these registration and mobilization regulations, and I am sure that the hon. member.? will agree with that sentiment. These measures were vitally necessary for war purposes. They helped Canada over many of our manpower difficulties, but they represented one of the features of wartime administration which a democratic public tolerate and even expect, but which the same public very properly feel is not in accord with the peacetime machinery necessary in the government of a free people.
I now lay on the table a copy of order in council P.C. 3449 of August 14, 1946, as referred to.

speechtext:
May I be permitted to give an oral answer to this question and then ask that it stand as an order for return in order that full details may be obtained? The information must be obtained from Regina

Questions as Orders jor Returns
and it will take some little time to get it. We may not get it before the end of the session, although I hope that will be possible.
The first question asks what work consisting of preliminary plans, survey parties and actual operations, has been done since January 1, 1946, in connection with (a) the projected diversion of part of the waters of the South Saskatchewan river at or near Elbow, Saskatchewan, including the erection of a dam? While I was in Regina a week or so ago I made inquiries and I found that the work that has been done so far this year consists merely of engineering work for the purpose of trying to locate a site at which a dam can be properly built. The difficulty is to find a foundation upon which to rest the dam, and up to that time a suitable site had not been found.
The next section of the question deals with the providing of a reservoir for waters in the Qu'Appelle valley. I think it will be known to the hon. member that there are several different reservoirs there in the form of dams at the end of lakes which either dry up or go down partly during the dry seasons in order to store some water. I do not know that any additions have been made in 1946 down to the present, although the detailed statement will show whether that is true or not. W e are locating dam sites along the north and south side of the Qu'Appelle for the purpose of storing water in order to let it corner down gradually during the summer rather than to rush away during the spring of the year.
The next part of the question deals with the elevation or the raising of the level of Long lake. I do not think any work was done there in 1946, although considerable work has been done during the last five or six years in an attempt to restore the levels of that lake. The complete restoration would be associated with whatever answer is given to question (a) having to do with the diversion of water down the Qu'Appelle if that is found necessary.
Section (d) deals with the conservation and increase of the waters of Watrous lake. I do not know that anything has been done in that regard in 1946, but detailed information will be provided. If this question is allowed to be made an order for return, full information will be given.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the house rose last evening we were discussing the government's -wheat policy for Canada. My remarks this morning will deal with two aspects of that policy, one the United Kingdom wheat agreement, and the other the government's general wheat policy as distinguished from the United Kingdom agreement.
My first point is that the United Kingdom agreement or contract is a complete reversal of traditional Liberal policy, whether you spell that Liberal with a capital "L" or a 63260-304
small "1", whether you use the word in the party political sense or in the wider sense as indicating the type of economy which the word is commonly used to describe. I shall take only a moment to illustrate what I mean by saying that this agreement is a departure from Liberal policy.
In recent years the government has committed itself to certain lines of policy aimed to promote trade and good will. For instance, in August, 1941, it agreed to the Atlantic charter. Clause 4 of that charter expresses the ideal, with due respect to existing obligationsof furthering the enjoyment by all States, great or small, victor or vanquished, of access, on equal terms, to the trade and to the raw materials of the world which are needed for their economic prosperity.
"On equal terms," it says. In this agreement we have a one-country arrangement which is not available to other countries. So the government's policy is a departure from that statement of policy laid down in the early years of the war.
Later the government approved the Bretton Woods agreement. In that agreement these words appear:
The fund has been projected to facilitate the establishment of a system of international payments that will maintain relative stability in exchange rates and will permit a multilateral trade pattern.
But in the United Kingdom agreement we have a bilateral trade pattern, and not a multilateral trade pattern.
In 1942 this government exchanged notes with the United States government along the same line. I will read just one clause from the exchange of notes of November 30, 1942.
Our two governments are prepared to cooperate in formulating a programme of agreed action, open to participation by all other countries of like mind, directed to the expansion, by appropriate international and domestic measures, of production, employment, and the exchange and consumption of goods, which are the material foundations of the liberty and welfare of all peoples; to the elimination of all forms of discriminatory treatment in international commerce; and to the reduction of tariffs and other trade barriers.
So the government of Canada in this United Kingdom agreement has departed not only from its traditional policy but from its agreements as expressed in these serious and well-considered statements of government policy. I need not take the time of the committee to read from more of these documents or from more statements by members of the government themselves. I shall content myself by referring to only one, the statement of the Minister of Finance on November 12 last

Supply-Trade and Commerce

when he was dealing with the question of withdrawing the government's tariff proposals. The government had planned some tariff increases and later decided to withdraw them, and on November 12, 1945, the Minister of Finance made this statement to the house:
The government has repeatedly expressed the view that in the interdependent world of today prosperity is indivisible, and that the prosperity of any nation cannot be long maintained without a restoration and expansion of international commerce.
We welcome every indication of a movement in the direction of reciprocal action to produce trade barriers.
' What I have said, Mr. Chairman, is that the government's wheat policy is a wide departure from those statements of what I believe and most of the Canadian people think were statements of wise policy.
Coming now to the agreement itself I said last night that we regard the agreement as a bad agreement. I shall try to summarize very briefly why we think that.
It is a bad agreement because it proposes to sell 160 million bushels of wheat to Britain at 50 cents a bushel below the world price. It is either a gift or it is an improvident trade arrangement. If it is a gift, let us say so. But if it is supposed to be an insurance against low prices in the future-if because we take less for our wheat to-day than it is worth Britain is expected to pay more for our wheat two years from now than the world price when it may be lower, I say that as an insurance that this will be done, it is valueless.
/ It is a bad bargain also because it will create / friction between Britain and Canada. , If in two or three years from now the world price of wheat is low and Britain does not come through with a higher price to us than the world price then is, we shall feel that she has renewed on this agreement. On the other hand, if two or three yearsfrom now, when the world price of wheat may be low, we press Britain to pay us more than the world price, she will feel that we are unreasonable. So I say that the proposal is altogether likely to create friction between this country and Britain.
The third reason why this is a bad bargain is that it will cause friction with other nations as well. It will invite criticism from the wheat-producing nations, because here we are selling wheat to the greatest wheat importer of the world at 50 cents a bushel below the world price. What are other wheat-producing nations to think of a policy of that kind.
It will also invite friction from the wheat consuming nations. Why? Because we are selling wheat to Britain at SI .55 a bushel when the world price is above 82 a bushel and we

do not offer our wheat to other countries at that low price. We are thus putting ourselves in a very unfavourable position to promote good will with the agricultural producing countries of the world on one hand and with the food-consuming countries on the other. This, Mr. Chairman, is the end of the government's policy of selling cheap wheat to the hungry nations of the world other than Britain, and it will be a handicap to us in trying to build up a market in all these other countries which so interpret this arrangement.
And this contract is a bad bargain because Britain can take this wheat at this low price, manufacture it into flour, and sell that flour at a lower price than flour that has been made by nations which have to pay $2 a bushel for their wheat. It is a bad bargain for this reason also-how Can Canada expect to sell the remainder of her wheat at $2 a bushel, the world price, if Britain is offering wheat, or flour made from wheat, at a price less than that? The tendency will be for that practice to drive down the world price and make difficult if not impossible the receiving by Canada of the present world price. I predict that in two years time, or a little more, this agreement will blow up, when the advantages to Britain are gone and when her own people will be wanting to get food at the world -price, as they have always wanted to, and when the world price will probably be lower than it is now.
Now, with respect to the government's wheat policy generally,-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Now with respect to the government's wheat policy generally, I make this criticism: it is not fair to the farmers, it is not fair to a quarter of the Canadian people, it is not fair-particularly-to those who are growing wheat. It is not fair because the price that is offered, $1.35, while there is a possibility that something more will be coming after the end of five years, there is no assurance that there will be. One dollar and thirty-five cents * is not a fair price for wheat to-day. It is not a "parity price", if I may use that hackneyed term. "Parity price", is the name given to a price which is supposed to express a fair price in relation to other things. The parity price now would be about $1.53, but $1.35 is all the farmers are assured, at a time when the world price is nearly half as high again as that. If the farmers of Canada cannot be assured of a parity price now, when the world price is high, what prospect is there of their being assured of parity price when the world price is low, as it is sure to be later on?	,
The government's policy during the last two or three years has been a policy generally of floors and ceilings. That has reduced the wide fluctuations of prices, and to that extent is gpod; it has raised the floors and lowered the ceilings. Now there is a modification of that policy. The government comes along with this price of $1.35, which as I have said is less than parity. The policy has been one of floors

and ceilings, but now it is one even more of a controlled economy; and when the government starts in to control the economy, then when things do not go right, or any inequity is brought about, the government has no one to blame but itself. This policy is not equitable. It does not assure equity to farmers, and this is one time when the government might have given them that assurance.
As I have said, the government's policy is one of no assurance of parity when the world price is high, and even less assurance when the world price is low. The government's policy is one of making agriculture carry the cost of the loss on this sale. It is not the nation that is carrying it. The nation's economy will suffer if it does not get as much for wheat as it might have got. But the price of the loss will be borne by the farmers. The government may say that the farmers are probably getting enough, but the fact is that this is a contribution by the farmers of Canada and not by the Canadian people as a whole. When you stop to think that on this one commodity the crop is sold at four different prices- wheat for flour at 78 cents, the so-called domestic price of $1.25, the British price of $1.55, and now the effort is being made to sell to other countries at over $2-you will realize that is very much of a hodge-podge, something which is most difficult to administer and does not work out equitably to the producers.
In closing I recognize that the wheat agreement is signed, signed by the officials of the United Kingdom and by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Whether it is good or bad, whether it is good in some respects and not as good as it might be in others, the fact remains that it has been signed and I am sure there is a desire on the part of everyone to carry it out. But with respect to the government's wheat price policies, other than those in the wheat agreement-the government, as I have said, has had an opportunity better than it has ever had to assure equity to agriculture. Whatever value $1.35 a bushel may have, it does not assure equity to agriculture at a time when equity could easily have been assured. If this policy, instead of declaring that the price will be $1.35 now for five years, had stipulated that it would be $1.55 now-such a price would for the time being have assured a reasonable degree of equity. But it does not do that. The government might have said that for five years it would agree that if the farmer's cost went up the price would go up and if the farmer's cost went down the price would go down; in other words, that it would adjust the price to the

Supply-Trade and Commerce
cost of things the farmers have to buy. That has not been done, and the opportunity to take a long step forward towards equity and justice and social and economic progress has been lost.
I suggest this to the government. The agreement has been signed, but the government can still say to the Canadian people: We will approve a price now of 81.55 a bushel and make it for five years, or three years or two years or one year, and if the farmer's cost goes up, as it. is likely to go up-because we cannot grant increases in costs to steel and labour; and all these other things without the farmer's cost going up-if the farmer's costs go up the price will be adjusted from year to year on the basis of these costs. Let it go higher if the costs are higher and lower if the costs are lower. If that were done we would have what every farmer has been wanting, and what every reasonable man in every other calling in the country has been wanting-equity, nothing more and nothing less. It might be difficult to assure that accurately in a free economy, but not so difficult in a controlled economy, or a semi-controlled economy as now. That is the only guarantee of real income stability to the farmer, and it has not been given. But it could be given, and I suggest that the government even yet agree to make the price $1.55 instead of $1.35 per bushel.

I have listened carefully both to the minister and to the leader of the opposition, and until the concluding sentences of the speech delivered by the latter gentleman I wondered what policy he would suggest. I may say at once that in regard to price I take a somewhat similar view, that at the present time the wheat agreement calls for the payment of $1.55 a bushel for the wheat that is sold to Britain and I believe that is nearer what we sometimes call a parity price. I believe the government would be well advised to consider this suggestion that, in the event of the costs of production rising for the next few years, as they will do largely because of the government's failure to maintain the ceilings, any difference there may be between what the farmer receives for his wheat and the increased cost of production should be made up out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
We have signed an agreement with Great Britain, and I take a view the very opposite to that of the leader of the opposition. I believe that, having signed that agreement, the British will not, to use the word which I believe the hen. gentleman used, renege on the deal. It has been the history of Great Britain, with all her faults and failings in the past, that she has lived up to her obligations,
and one thing that has often been said is that the Britisher's word is his bond. I am convinced that this agreement will be fulfilled to the full by any British government which happens to be in power for the next several years.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit a question? I understood him to say he considered that parity was somewhere around $1.50 or $1.55. I think it was fairly well admitted that prior to the increase in implement prices and labour which has recently taken place, parity would probably be about $1.41 or $1.42-somewhere around there. The point I wanted to raise was this. The situation has again changed materially in relation to, say, implement prices by the fact that the ten per cent exchange adjustment has been made, which will result in implements coming from the United States being sold at ten per cent less. I am given to understand that a combine is selling at $160 less than before that change was made, which means that all implements made in this country will have to come down too. What we call parity, adjusted from day to day, would be a very difficult thing to apply to wheat, and what we are presuming of course is that for a four-year period parity will probably work out at what we figured it at during the last four or five years-$1.41 rather than $1.55-and it is on that basis that the discussion took place, whether the advance should be $1.35 or $1.40. The farmers organization argued that to put it at parity it should be $1.40, and that is parity over a long period, not a week or a month. It will be agreed by most persons that a parity figure that should be finally used in criticism of the agreement as it works out would be rather a four-year parity than a four weeks or a four months parity.

What I had in mind was that the cost of living, according to the figures of the bureau of statistics, has increased by five points in the last three months, and I was making the point that if this increase continues, an adjustment should be made. If what the minister says is correct and parity over the period of the agreement should be in the neighbourhood of $1.40 or $1.35, or whatever it may be, of course that would be a different story, but the point I think I made quite clearly was that if costs of production and costs of living continue to rise, a compensatory adjustment should be made out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada. We cannot go back to Great Britain and say they will have to pay more, or we would be doing what the leader of the
Supply-Trade and Commerce

opposition thinks Britain might do under other circumstances, when he suggested they might be inclined to renege on the deal.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

You used the word

I hope, Mr. Chairman, you are considering these interruptions in connection with my time, though I do not expect to take forty minutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We shall not insist on the matter of time, and anyway we are in committee. What I want to point out is that under the floor price measure-that is not the proper name, but it will do-we stated to the house that $200,000,000 was being provided for the purpose of taking care of any adjustments in connection with what might be known as parity on other farm products. At the same time we stated to the house that similar arrangements would be made if necessary, through the wheat board, in connection with grain. I just want to point out that provision is made in another way.

I am glad to know that provision is made should circumstances arise making it necessary. I was not aware of that, and I doubt very much whether other hon. members were aware that this was the interpretation which might be placed upon the previous statement made by the minister.
I was amazed to hear the leader of the opposition accuse the government of attempting by this agreement to end the policy of selling cheap wheat to countries other than Britain. Surely if the farmers of western Canada have suffered at all they suffered particularly during the years from 1930 to 1939

or later from the policy of selling cheap wheat. Why, we know in western Canada that on one occasion at' Fort William wheat went down to 38 cents a bushel for No. 1 northern, which meant at the country points in my own constituency, for example, that No. 1 northern was worth 20 cents a bushel. If that is what this agreement ends, then I am all for this agreement, and I am surprised to hear the leader of the opposition or anyone else in the house suggest that the agreement ends the policy of selling cheap wheat to countries other than Britain. I hope it does end that policy for all time.
Let me comment briefly upon another provision which I regret is in the agreement, because I do think it leads to a tremendous amount of misunderstanding. I refer to the clause which permits Great Britain to sell or otherwise dispose of the wheat. I wish we could get a fuller explanation of what that clause means. But I bear in mind that very recently Britain herself surrendered 200,000,000 tons of foodstuffs to feed the starving people of western Europe, particularly the people of her former enemy, Germany. If you look up the statistics you will find that practically half a billion dollars was spent on food by Britain, not for resale to the distressed nations but in order to relieve starvation on the continent of Europe; half a billion dollars of the money of the British taxpayers was spent for that purpose. I hope this clause in the agreement is an indication of an intention to continue that kind of humanitarian policy.
Now I want to say to the Minister of Agriculture that even if conversion comes late I am glad it does come. I look back over the years before the war and during the war when those of us in this party advocated agreements of this type, and I remember the minister rising in his place and denouncing such agreements, stating that open market trading set a price which was fair and reasonable for the commodity sold. I did not have time to look through all the records, but I recall that in 1939, for example -and I chose a year before the war-in foreshadowing legislation following the Turgeon report, the minister said at page 1037 of Hansard for that year:
. . . we intend to introduce legislation which will carry out as far as possible the recommendations of the Turgeon commission, which were:
First, that the government should remain out of the grain trade and our wheat should be marketed by means of the futures market system.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
I shall read the other two paragraphs, though they have little bearing:
Second, that the grain exchange should be placed under proper supervision.
Third, that encouragement be given to the creation of cooperative marketing associations or pools.
Then in explanation the minister went on:
We cannot agree that there is likely to be permanency to any system of marketing farm products which is based upon price fixing. We prefer to embark upon a policy which will lead to costs of production and standards of product which will invite a paying market for all our farm products.
I am pleased indeed that the minister has come to the conclusion that another policy is better than the one he outlined at that time. May I also add that I think this policy is in conformity with what is being done by other countries. After all, we have to view realistically the situation in which we find ourselves, and when realism demands a change of policy then that change must be made.
I think the wheat agreement is a very important step in the attempt to achieve stability in the price of wheat to the western grower. I have just come back from western Canada. As the minister indicated, he also came back a day or two ago. We had a national convention, at. which I met a good many representative farmers other than the delegates who were there. Being interested in this wheat agreement, and having given some approval to it before to-day, naturally I was interested in finding out what was the reaction on the part of the people whom I have known for a good many years. I found, as the minister found, that while the western farmer thinks, as I indicated earlier, that the price to him now Should be higher, none the less he feels that this agreement makes for some stability in the production and marketing of wheat, and that he is now relieved from the dangers from which he suffered during the period immediately following the last war, when 'he saw the price of wheat drop from nearly $3 a bushel down to slightly over SI a bushel in approximately twelve months. And he realizes that if he can get a stable market at a stable price which is adequate to maintain a reasonable and decent standard of living, in the long run he will be better off than if he took a high price now and a low price two years from now. And I say that so far as it is designed to achieve stability, it should meet with this parliament's approval. Regardless of what Great Britain may pay in the last two years, it guarantees an initial price of $1.35 a bushel for the period of the agreement. And at the end of that period I believe we shall be able to look back and
say that, in all certainty, this agreement did give a measure of stability, and perhaps protected the farmers-as I shall show later on -from some of the dangers inherent in the present world situation. This of course is vitally important to the Canadian farmer, and may be even more important in the later years of the agreement.
But while we are dealing with our overseas customers, the farmer is entitled to expect that the government will set the same price .for our millers on the wheat used in the domestic market. I believe that is the universal opinion of western wheat growers, and I suggest the government would be well advised to reconsider that phase of its policy. After all, an increase from approximately 78 cents to $1.35 per bushel, even if it were carried into the price of a loaf of bread, would not mean more than a rise of one cent in the price of that loaf in this country. While bread is a very important commodity, I do not think that under any circumstances our farmers should be called upon as a group in any way to assist in doing something that the whole of Canada should do. Therefore I suggest that that phase of government policy should be reconsidered.
During the war farmers were called upon to produce under great difficulties, and to make great sacrifices. We should not now ask them to continue to make sacrifices. They are entitled now to a price, and a guarantee in price, which will give them a proper return for their labour and enable them to live as well as those who live decently and well in our urban centres. And when I refer to a proper standard of living I am thinking of the standard of those who live decently and well in urban centres.
The price at which our wheat is being sold to Great Britain at the present time is $1.55. Again the criticism is made that this is below the United States price. I believe that yesterday the Minister of Agriculture was clear and also wise in placing before the committee the fact that it was the United States price we were talking about, not what is sometimes called the world price. But whatever the United States price is to-day, it may well be that during the course of this agreement there may be a spectacular fall in world prices, which, without the protection of an agreement of this kind, might prove disastrous to the farmers of Canada. But, as I warned a moment ago, if the cost of production rises there must be some compensatory payment to the farmers of Canada, apart altogether from the British agreement.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

What the farmers need, and what we in this party have always urged, is a parity price. I do not know how hon. members would define that expression, because there are a good many definitions of it. But the one I always keep in mind is this, that a parity price is one which bears direct relationship to other costs in the economy-costs of production, costs of living, and the like. I admit immediately that this involves a considerable amount of economic and social planning.
This particular feature of the matter, namely the parity price and a decent standard of living, is important. We must not overlook the fact that while the government guarantees to take all the wheat delivered in the crop year
1946-47, after that time the farmers may be put on a quota of deliveries amounting to fourteen bushels per seeded acre, if and when required.
Authorized.

Yes, authorized. If that should occur it means of course that the returns from wheat may be lower than would maintain the standard of living to which I have referred. I know that the average production of wheat on our western farms over a period of years is slightly over 15 bushels to the acre-15 - 7 I think it is. Perhaps if we were to deduct the seed, the amount that is fed, and averaged the remainder over the entire area, the average might be about 14 bushels to the acre.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It actually is.

I want to be fair in my discussion of this particular phase of the matter. Obviously-and the interjection of the Minister of Agriculture when the leader of the opposition was speaking emphasizes it -there is no further use for a Winnipeg grain exchange. To keep it open to play with rye, with coarse grains, or even with a surplus of 'wheat, would, I think, mean that all we were doing was maintaining an institution which has outlived any usefulness. We know perfectly well that in other countries exchanges of the type of our grain exchange are being closed. One of the greatest in the world, the cotton exchange in Great Britain, was closed permanently not long ago. I believe the Liverpool grain exchange will not reopen.
The success of this agreement will depend upon the grain situation in the world in a few years, and in this respect I think the agreement may be a valuable protection for our western farmers. Canada's exports of machinery alone, as placed on record the other day by the hon. member for Melfort,

indicate the extent to which mechanization is going on in countries which were not mechanized before the war.
W'hen I was in Great Britain in the autumn of 1944 I had the privilege of flying from Prestwick to London. Upon arriving there I remarked that, having been born in that country and having lived there until I was about twenty-one years of age, and knowing the rural districts of England rather well- because all my relatives were engaged in agriculture-I had been amazed while flying over that country to see the degree of cultivation which had taken place. I was amazed to see that there were actually combines operating in some of the fields. When on a subsequent occasion I made these observations to a member of the British government he said, "Great Britain is now the most highly mechanized agricultural community in the whole world." One finds it difficult to believe that, but the figures were produced to show that with their tractors and their high-powered farm equipment they had become at least one of the most highly mechanized agricultural countries in the world. In the same autumn we crossed parts of Europe and saw the difference there. For instance, in France we saw farmers cultivating their land with walking-ploughs pulled by a cow and a horse hitched together-using the most primitive methods of cultivation. And yet we know that even under these circumstances, prior to the war France was able to export wheat- and indeed, exported considerable quantities of it in some years. But now, with the feverish attempt to grow cereals in order to feed the starving population of Europe, these countries are mechanizing to an extent undreamed of a few years ago. We know what Russia was able to do in a few years of mechanization. In the semi-arid regions of North Africa-and wheat is a semi-arid plant -they are placing large new acreages under cultivation and using new and high-powered machinery. Australia and the Argentine republic will not in all likelihood suffer from another severe drought in the next few years and we may again see accumulations of wheat pile up. This agreement would then protect our western farmers to an extent that, may be very valuable to them in the years to come.
As the minister said yesterday, the records show that this will mean that for the four years we shall be guaranteed a market for sixty per cent more wheat than Great Britain was buying before the war. I have not looked it up, but I think my memory serves me correctly when I say that the banner year before the war in our exports of wheat to the United Kingdom was around1 102 million

Supply-Trade and Commerce
bushels, although I am not quite sure of that figure. But I do know that the statement is correct that this will give our western farmer an assured market for an average of sixty per cent more than we exported to Great Britain before the war. This would be a great advantage to us should surpluses accumulate.
May I remark to the leader of the opposition and to my friends of the Winnipeg Free Press that they are clinging to an outworn philosophy of trade when they follow the principle of laissez faire. There is no question about it that we shall never come back again to the old methods of trade. Governments will not allow their basic supplies to remain in the hands of speculative interests who are concerned not with the welfare of the people of the world but only with the making of profits out of the needs of the community.
In Europe, which is our principal customer, governments of all types are engaged in protecting their people against the fluctuations brought about by speculation. I know that those of us who believe that are often accused of pinning our faith to what is called bilateralism. I do not think this is bilateralism. A bilateral agreement would mean that if we were to sell Great Britain 160 or 150 or 140 million bushels of wheat at a given price, we would undertake to take from Great Britain at the same time an amount of British goods which would substantially cancel the value of the goods we were sending to.Britain. That, substantially, would be a bilateral agreement. To my mind an agreement of this kind may actually break open the markets of the world and lead to a new form of multilateral trade. That is what I hope and have always hoped, and that is what I believe will happen. As long as we have socialist governments-and they are going to continue in power and grow in power across the world-they will not allow their people to become the victims of speculation in essential commodities.
I should like to note one feature of the agreement which may be of value to us and to the world. Provision is made for entry into a world wheat agreement if and when it can be reached. I hope that such a world agreement can be reached, because it would be beneficial not only to Canada but to all the world. Our government has been forced by the trend of events to consider and accept an agreement of this kind and I know it will be forced further along this path.
If we want to maintain, not only adequate farm prices but an adequate standard: of living for our workers, we shall have to have more and more not of regimentation but of the
kind of democratic control that is needed foi our economy. This means that we shall have to plan our economy more closely than ever. At the moment these agreements are not sufficiently inclusive of Canadian products. We want to maintain high levels of employment, which depend upon high standards of living on the farm. High standards of living on the farm depend upon high levels of employment. But an over-all plan could do these things, so that an agreement of this sort would not fail.
I do not want to say much more, except that with the qualifications I have given I welcome this agreement. I believe I am speaking for the great majority of my supporters and the supporters of this movement when I say that to the extent to which it will achieve stability in this great commodity which we produce in such vast quantities, to that extent it will be beneficial. No one can foretell the future, but the value or otherwise of this agreement will be known in the course of the next four years.
I am prepared to say that if the government makes the provisions that I have mentioned for necessary adjustments, it will be beneficial. Before I sit down I must say I am certain that the present British government which negotiated it, or any successor to that government will honour the signatures to this agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Just before this item stands I should like to take this opportunity to answer a question asked by the hon. member for Battle River, and also a suggested question by the leader of the opposition. The hon. member for Battle River asked whether shippers and exporters are being paid commissions by the Canadian wheat board.
I want to set the minister straight. I did not refer to shippers and exporters; I asked about brokers and commission merchants.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I think I will cover it in my answer. My understanding was that the inquiry had reference to shippers and exporters. Shippers and exporters have not been paid any commission since the market was closed in 1943. The brokers and exporters were paid commissions on work they did in connection with the wheat board up until a year ago, when these payments were discontinued. Where purchases for export are made through brokers and exporters I am informed that the usual commission is charged the purchaser, but there is no charge on the wheat board and of course no charge directly or indirectly on the wheat producer.
As to the 14-bushel restriction on the authorized acreage, which is between 21 and 22 million acres, there are no restrictions on delivery in 1945-46 and no restrictions on delivery in 1946-47. The hon. gentleman has not read the whole statement:
In determining the prices for these two crop years, 1948-49 and 1949-50, the United Kingdom government will have regard to any difference between the prices paid under this agreement in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years and the world prices for wheat in the 1946-47 and 194748 crop years.
That was to give expression to a matter that was fully discussed as between Canada and Gi eat Britain, and we on behalf of the government-that is, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and myself-suggested that in view of the fact that Great Britain was going to get wheat at some margin below the world price in 1946-47, they should be prepared, no matter whether wheat is below or above $1.25 or even above $1.55, to take into consideration any advantage that they get by obtaining 
wheat at a low level during these first two years. Without any reservations whatsoever those with whom we were discussing it came right back and said, "That is absolutely fair. We would have no reason for refusing to do it, and we ought to do it." They put that in these words, in order to express fully their intention, and I am in full agreement with the leader of the C.C.F. when he says that our negotiations and dealings with the British, right from the beginning of the war, have been such as to indicate that anything they put in writing in this form will be carried out, either by the present government or by any other government that may be in power. I am quite sure that will be done.
You admit they will take it into consideration, but no actual basis is set put.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No; the actual basis will have to be established in the light of the facts as they are at the time. Still I am satisfied that the British would say this: "If we got the wheat at 20 or 30 cents a bushel less than the world price during that period, certainly we are prepared to negotiate a satisfactory basis." I do not think they would say they would consider the difference to the extent of 100 per cent and go on that basis; it would depend on the number of bushels they were buying. One fact has been missed in all these discussions. On an average the British buy 200,000,000 bushels a year. This 160,000.000 bushels does not feed them; they buy 200,000,000 bushels a year to feed themselves, and this year it is proved, and shown by all the records that have been put out by the united nations, that Britain must have 195.000,000 bushels. Britain was insistent on buying 180,000,000 bushels from us. They were quite prepared to put that right in the agreement; but in the early stages of the negotiations we did not know whether we were going to have 180,000,000 bushels to sell them, so we said we did not want to put something into the agreement we might not be able to carry out, so as a result somebody might say we had broken the agreement. We got down to a figure representing the quantity we were certain we could supply. I think it is most difficult to anticipate that Britain, requiring 200,000,000 bushels of wheat and having purchased 160,000.000 bushels, is going to sell some of the 160,000.000 bushels that she has bought for $1.55 and buy some more at $2. I would begin to wonder about this hard trading of the British if they did that. Therefore I do not place very much importance in the argument which has been advanced along those lines. On this other point they have

Supply-Trade and Commerce
definitely said, "We know we are getting the wheat at a lower price, in the first year in any case. We do not know what is going to happen in the second year." If we were to get a crop of 550,000,000 bushels, as it looked three weeks ago-I would say twenty-five per cent has been cut off since then-there is no doubt in my mind that the price of wheat would have gone down in the second year of this contract, not the third. All these conditions develop as we go along, and the British say that taking into consideration what may happen throughout the period of the agreement, if they get an advantage in the first two years they are going to take that into consideration in whatever price is negotiated for the last two years.

speechtext: May I ask the minister just one question about this 160,000,000 bushels coming from Canada and purchased by Britain? Will the minister say all that wheat will be consumed in Britain?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Well, I will not say all of it will be consumed in Britain, because I would expect that what was mentioned here this morning may happen again, and provision is written into the contract for it to happen. One of the objections to this contract was that the united nations may come along and say that Britain cannot have this much wheat, in order that someone else may not starve. It has been written right into the contract that if Britain desires to give up some of her wheat in order to feed somebody else, she can give it away if she likes. On the same premise she can sell it at a lower price than $1.55, or she can dispose of it in any way she sees fit in order to help feed the world. But when it comes to the question of Britain disposing of it just as a matter of making money, there is no way in which she can do that unless wheat goes away below what it is to-day.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to repeat the arguments advanced this morning by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) or the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross), both of whom set forth clearly the position of the opposition in respect of this agreement.
May I say ait the outset that having regard to the vast extent of the operations of the Canadian wheat board, the time has come for the board to give a full accounting
of its transactions between 1937 and 1945. This is of general interest and of general demand throughout western Canada. So far no statement of the kind has been secured from the board.
In 1943 an action was initiated by Arthur Henry Oatway in Manitoba against the Canadian wheat board asking for an accounting in respect of certain years. Application to the courts was made on behalf of the wheat board that the action be set aside on the ground that no action lay as against the wheat board in that it was an emanation of the crown. The application was dismissed by the judge who heard the motion. The wheat board appealed to the court of appeal in Manitoba, and that court, by a majority of one, allowed the appeal and held that proceedings against the Canadian wheat board for an accounting could not be taken. An appeal was carried to the Supreme Court of Canada, at which time the government took an attitude which I think is totally inexcusable. An order in council was passed denying anyone the right to ask for an accounting from the wheat board. In other words that order in council assured silence in regard to what actually took place between 1937 and 1944. I say the time has come when a complete statement should be given-not an ex parte statement such as at the present time-by the wheat board setting forth in detail its conduct, and also subjecting itself and its officials to full examination.
There are various ways in which our wheat may be disposed of. I am surprised to see the change of attitude on the part of the government in adopting a bilateral agreement, because for the past several years the attitude of the government has been that multilateral agreements are the only salvation for world peace. As a matter of fact that was the principle behind the formation of the food and agricultural organization of the united nations. It was one of the main principles in the Atlantic charter, and of the united nations enunciated at San Francisco.
Another means of'disposing of our wheat would be to build up in this country a population which will consume much of the Canadian wheat which to-day must be shipped to Europe if it is to find a market. Our position in western Canada is that we have to ship our wheat, bacon and other products four or five thousand miles to get a market among the millions of people in Europe and elsewhere. I believe the time has come when this parliament should face the issue, and that instead of our continuing to find markets abroad a policy of selective immigration should be institiuted, thereby bringing a larger market to our own country.

I am not alone in that point of view. For Canada to follow the course which apparently she is following, the country being maintained for Canadians or the descendants of those who originally came here, is to make this country the target for any future aggressor nation. We are not developing the resources we have and we cannot develop them if we follow the present system of simply keeping within Canada the people who are here, subject to the present tremendous exodus of native-born Canadians to the United States. By continuing that policy the government will be making Canada's position such that aggressor-minded countries which have not ample supplies of food and natural resources will look to Canada with envious eyes.
We have the land; we have the resources to be developed. According to the Minister of Agriculture, speaking in February in Regina- and the government has been strangely silent about this matter since the beginning of the session-the solution for many of our problems would be for Canada to have a population sufficiently large to consume at least sixty per cent of our wheat crop. That was his statement in Regina, and he added that western Canada itself needs six million people more than it has to-day if it is to utilize the natural resources available for development.
The present situation in Canada demands an aggressive policy of immigration, strictly selective and controlled to the end that the numbers brought in here shall be able to maintain themselves and not put people in our country out of work. I know there are those who say we cannot have that to-day because of a lack of transportation. Well, sir, none of our ancestors came over on the Queen Mary. They came on whatever ships were available, and people are willing to come to-day, however lowly the ship facilities, from all parts of the world, good citizens, to help us solve a problem which can be solved only if we have a larger population.

As I said a moment ago, multilateral agreements among the nations of the world was the basis of the food and agriculture organization of the united nations, and yet Canada is the first nation to depart from the principle we accepted at San Francisco, namely, multilateral rather than bilateral agreements so that discrimination, unfairness and potential economic warfare shall not come to the world again.
So far as this agreement is concerned I would repeat the criticisms of the hon. member for Souris set out in the most able and constructive address he gave to-day, and I should like to add to them. The agreement is unfair to the Canadian farmer; it is unfair to the producer. It is said that by selling now for fifty cents per bushel lower, after a period of years we shall have built up a credit in gratitude and as a result the nations favoured will grant higher prices when commodity prices and the wheat prices come down. That is the excuse that is given to-day. Again I should like to quote from the Winnipeg Free Press, which has always had the ear of the government. It gives the reason as follows:
The Canadian farmers are being denied the going price not in behalf of British consumers but because of domestic price control.
In other words, the excuse is that we are going to help Britain; the reason is that the government is endeavouring to maintain price control here in Canada.

Can we complain that Denmark has taken a large share of our bacon market in the old country through a bilateral agreement with Britain when we ourselves are discriminating against other nations by making this bilateral agreement? Canada gave the lead in bilateral agreements, and now we are starting to reap in this country, in the agreement with Denmark respecting bacon, what we have sown under this agreement.
Can there be any justification for Britain receiving under this agreement some 57,000,000 bushels of wheat more than she ordinarily purchases from Canada, and having it for sale, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Souris, being able to place that wheat in competition with Canadian wheat on the markets of the world? If there is to be a subsidy in favour of th'e mother country- and I am not raising any objection to that at the moment; if Britain is to be permitted to purchase wheat from us at 50 cents a bushel less than the world price, that subsidy should not be placed on the shoulders of our wheat-producing farmers but on the people of Canada as a whole.
I come to another criticism, and this was referred to by the hon. member for Souris. Is there any excuse whatsoever for the wheat board retaining twenty cents a bushel of the farmer's price this year for a period of five years and holding it undistributed, without interest just holding it back from the farmer as it has been held back for the last few years? It is in effect a forced loan to the government from the farmers of this country who are producing wheat amounting to approximately 8108,000,000. This twenty cents a bushel which is being held back by the government should be placed in a trust account, and out of it should be evolved a system of crop insurance to the end that there will be available to the farmers of this country legislation for which they have asked for so many years.
Finally, the prices in 1948, 1949 and 1950 of SI .25 and SI a bushel will, if past experience recurs, become the price at which wheat will be sold at that time, even though but for this agreement the price determined by the world price would have been higher. As was pointed out by the leader of the C.C.F. party and my hon. leader, the prices of $1 and 81.25 three or four years hence are just guesswork, with no regard to prices being on the rise for the things the farmer has to buy and no regard for parity prices in a period of two or three years.
The minister may ask, how are we going to look ahead that far? I understand that in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, and in his own department too, quite a collection of experts have been working for some time, more or less drafting the future and indicating what may be expected by

industry, agriculture and the like, so that they will be able to anticipate for a considerable period in advance what prices will be for commodities and what supply of commodities will be available.
Those in the main are my criticisms of this agreement. I am bound to say that our criti- cism at this time is almost meaningless and futile, because we are handed a completed fact, an agreement that was not the result of cooperation between the government of Canada and the great wheat producers of this country or t'heir representatives, but an agreement that was entered into at the request of the Canadian government and not at the solicitation of the British government. Only the other day I read that Mr. Strachey, I think it was, said that the agreement was not consummated as a result of the request of the British government but that the Canadian government gave the lead.
Let me say this in conclusion with regard to bilateral agreements. The Canadian federation of agriculture has opposed this type of agreement. Bilateral agreements cannot but lead to the arousing of antagonisms amongst other nations. It is in direct conflict not only with the Atlantic charter but with the whole framework of the united nations organization. The Canadian government and the minister, himself a tribune of this house for multilateral agreements, have become the first to return to economic nationalism and to the type of agreements such as this, which culminated in the last war.
