I am net following the course set by the hon. member who has just taken
his seat. I shall try to talk on the wheat agreement, which I think is the subject before us this afternoon.
The hon. member for Lake Centre made the argument that we shall probably have difficulty in exporting our wheat in the future, and that one of the best ways to find a market for Canadian wheat available for export is to bring immigrants into Canada, and so have a market here. He went on to quote what the Minister of Agriculture said in Regina. According to that quotation, apparently the Minister of Agriculture advocated that we should have six million immigrants. But we need each year to export something like 280 million bushels of wheat:	twelve million
people in Canada to-day consume 60 million bushels; another six million would consume an additional 30 million bushels; and we could still have 250 million bushels of wheat that we would have to find a market for. If we want to bring to Canada sufficient people to eat all the wheat we can grow here we would need to have at least another fifty-six million immigrants, and I do not believe that even the hon. member for Lake Centre would advocate immigration to the extent of an additional fifty-six million persons.
The hon. member went on to say that this was a bilateral agreement and as such was an impediment to multilateral agreements being eonsumated in the future. I should like to read part of clause 7 of the agreement, which states:
Having in mind the general purposes which this agreement is designed to serve, the two governments have agreed that its terms and conditions shall be subject to any modification or amendment which may be necessary to bring it into conformity with any international agreements . . .
No one in this house has questioned the integrity of the British government or the Canadian government in making this agreement, and the agreement states that it will be moulded in the future to any multilateral agreements which may be made.
I agree with the leader of this group (Mr. Coldwell) who stated that we in this party welcome the agreement. In my opinion if it is the best possible agreement the government could make under the circumstances, then it is all that any reasonable person can expect. The guaranteed price for wheat in the last year of this agreement is $1 per bushel. I am not going to try to prophesy whether wheat is likely to fall to that amount, but everyone in this house knows that a dollar a bushel is not sufficient for the Canadian farmer, and if in the future we are going to base the Canadian domestic price wholly or mainly on the price we
Supply-Trade and Commerce

receive for wheat on the markets of the world, I am certain that we shall soon get back to a dollar a bushel. If we are to find and maintain markets for Canadian exports of wheat we must be willing and able at all times to receive sufficient products to give the nations that are buying our wheat enough Canadian currency to pay for it. International agreements for food commodities, even if they cover the available supplies of all commodities for export, are doomed to failure if the exporting countries are not prepared to take .imports from the countries which are buying those exports. So, if we are to have international trade as a two-way stream, it is not only necessary that agreements be made as the agreement with Britain has been made, but the government must follow a policy of increasing continuously the well-being of the Canadian people so that we shall always have a standard of living sufficiently high to be able to purchase the imports which other nations wish to send us in exchange for our wheat.
In 1943 the initial price for wheat was set at $1.25 per bushel. Since that time partcipa-tion payments are being made to the extent of twelve cents a bushel, making the price for the 1943 crop $1.37 per bushel. For the 1945 crop farmers received an initial payment of $1.25; they are to be given another ten cents. The price for wheat sold in 1945, apart from any payment which may be made at the end of the 1949 crop year, will be $1.35 per bushel. The price which the farmer is guaranteed for 1945 is two cents a bushel less than the price he received for 1943. The cost of producing wheat in the year 1945 as compared with 1943 had certainly gone up. The Minister of Agriculture told us this morning that this spring, before the increases in costs took place, a parity price was $1.41 or $1.42 a bushel. Since that time the cost of living to the farmer, the costs of things he has to buy which go into his production, have been increasing tremendously. The cost of living index from March to July jumped five points. Gasoline within that time went up two cents a gallon, machinery went up 12i per cent, a host of other commodities have risen in price, and prices continue to rise. According to the financial experts of the government, who should know, we are still in a period of inflation, and there is going to be more inflation.
I say therefore that if the farmer is to be guaranteed stable real income his prices must be adjusted from time to time as the costs of production change. It would seem to me that $1.55 is a reasonable and fair price at

this time. I would say, too, that price should
be adjusted as costs to farmers change from, time to time.
Does the hon. member mean that if costs of production to the farmer decrease he would advocate a reduction in the present price under the agreement to the farmer for these two years?

What the Canadian farmer wants is a high level of national income; he wishes, out of that high level of income, his fair share, and if his costs go down to the extent that if he received a previous price he would be getting more than his fair share of the national income, the farmer would agree, and I would agree, that his prices might be adjusted downward as the costs to him decreased.
That does not answer the question.

That answers the question, I believe. I want to take a few figures based on what I consider reasonable assumptions. The figure $1.55, in my area, would bring a price of something like $1.35 to the farmer. The average size of farm in my district is 325 cultivated acres; the number of acres of field crops is 204 on the average. The average yield is eleven bushels of wheat, which would give the farmer each year on the average 2,244 bushels. If one takes 244 bushels as a reasonable amount of seed for seeding 204 acres the farmer has 2,000 bushels of wheat to sell. If he gets $1.35 at the elevator he has $2,700 to provide for all the expenses of farming, which include machinery, gasoline, interest and taxes and depreciation, and also the cost of maintaining his family. I say that $2,700 as a gross income is not too high.
Do you think that is high enough for 325 acres?

I am not saying that is necessarily high enough, but surely it is the lowest average that should be tolerated. During this session, in another part of the building, I have heard it said that a worker needs $1,750 a year as a basic minimum. I have not yet heard anyone say that is too high. I say then that if $1,750 is a reasonable basic minimum for workers, below which none should be allowed to go, $2,700 gross income is certainly a very reasonable average income and one which farmers should have as of right, because that figure means, the way averages work out, that most farmers will get even less. That is, the average farmer would get, if the price of wheat were at this time $1.55 a bushel, the gross income I have indicated.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Our national income was running at eleven billions or eleven and three-quarter billions at the peak of wartime production, which on the basis of the 1941 census gave an average income per capita in Canada of about $1,000. The cash income of farmers in 1945-and there were 3-15 million persons engaged in agriculture- the total cash income, I say, was $1,685 million or a per capita cash income for people living on farms cf $530. The average income in Canada is $1,000. The average cash income for farming is $530, and out of that $530 the farmers of Canada have to pay all expenses of producing the products they sell. The net income in 1945 of 3-15 million people engaged in agriculture in Canada was just a little over one billion dollars. The average per capita net income was $330 for people engaged in agriculture. Surely any reasonable person, and in this I include most members sitting opposite, will agree that $330 per capita net income for farmers is too low with an average national income, I repeat, of $1,000.
I welcome the wheat agreement. I think it provides a start for the making of international agreements when there is in the agreement a clause which provides that the agreement will be made to conform to international agreements. In view of the costs to farmers, which have increased this year, I, along with the united farmers' organization, Saskatchewan branch, say that $1.55 is the lowest price that should prevail at this time. Further, I say that if costs increase next year, as it appears they will, then next year that price should be adjusted upwards to take care of the increased costs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I do not intend to detain the house more than a few minutes, but I think I should say a word in regard to the wheat agreement. I too have been in the west and I was surprised at the apparent unanimity of approval of this agreement among the people to whom I spoke.
There is one thing I should like to say at the very outset, however, before I discuss the agreement itself. I am repeating what I have said on more than one occasion and also the representations I have made to the government from time to time. I think that consideration should be given to raising the price at which the wheat board sells wheat to the domestic millers for domestic consumption from $1.25 to $1.55. I feel I cannot urge the government too strongly to give consideration to that change being made at the very earliest possible date.
I wish also to say a word in regard to the argument that there is inflation at the present time, that there will be more inflation, and therefore there is no use in trying to introduce
any element of stability into the situation. That argument carries my mind back to the period after the first great war when there was a time of uncertainty and inflation very much the same as has followed this second great war, the period in which we find ourselves today. At that time prices were rising and the same argument was heard-that wheat prices should be permitted to go almost sky high, and that it was in the interests of the farmers that they should do so. Then we went through that period. Those of us who were interested in farming in western Canada at that time came to believe, and I am sure the committee will agree with me, that the fact that prices to the farmer were permitted to go sky high and out of control actually injured the farmer in the long run more than it helped. It caused the prices of the things he had to buy, land and everything else, also to rise. He went into debt on that basis; then when prices dropped he was left in an almost bankrupt position, because he had been misled by what had happened during the period when prices went out of control. I think if we are not careful we may be in for a somewhat similar period soon, though I hope and think it will not be as bad; but after that movement takes place, if it does, there will be another reversal.
It seems to me what the farmer wants is not that sort of thing, but a certain measure of stability. That is wanted not only by the farmers but by the whole world. My mind goes back to the nineteen thirties, when the prices of primary products the world over, wheat, wool, meat and so on, went down to ruinous levels. Some people thought that would help the consuming countries of Europe, but that was not their experience. The very fact that their customers were getting ruinous prices for the goods they had to sell meant that their markets for manufactured goods were destroyed. For example, I am sure one of the things which greatly contributed to the rise to power of Hitler was the fact that Germany's markets abroad were destroyed, unemployment was created on a large scale, and those unemployed men found themselves in the nazi party.
I had the privilege of attending the international monetary conference at Bretton Woods in 1944, where I had a chance of talking to the representatives of Great Britain, for example, in regard to their attitude toward cheap wheat, cheap wool, cheap meat and so on. Their attitude was that they did not want that situation to occur again; that when the primary producing countries of South America, Australia, New Zealand and North America could) not get reasonable prices for their products it had a ruinous
Supply-Trade and Commerce

effect upon the export manufacturing industries of Great Britain itself. So there was general agreement that what the world needed was international agreement to provide some stability of price levels; and in this wheat agreement we are just recognizing that feeling and trying to fit ourselves into that general world picture.
I should like to read to the committee from article VII of the resolutions of the international monetary conference in regard to that matter, because I think we cannot give too much attention to this trend) in world affairs looking to security and stability for the workers and farmers of the world. Here is what it says:
Whereas, in article I of the articles of agreement of the international monetary fund it is stated that one of the principal purposes of the fund is to facilitate the expansion and balanced growth of international trade, and to contribute thereby to the promotion and maintenance of high levels of employment and real income and to the developmennt of the productive resources of all members as primary objectives of economic policy;
Whereas, it is recognized that the complete attainment of this and other purposes and objectives stated in the agreement cannot be achieved through the instrumentality of the fund alone; therefore
The united nations monetary and financial conference recommends:
To the participating governments that, in addition to implementing the specific monetary and financial measures which were the subject of this conference, they seek, with a view to creating in the field of international economic relations conditions necessary for the attainment of the purposes of the fund and of the broader primary objectives of economic policy, to reach agreement as soon as possible on ways and means whereby they may best:
(1)	reduce obstacles to international trade and in other ways promote mutually advantageous international commercial relations;
(2)	bring about the orderly marketing of staple commodities at prices fair to the producer and consumer alike;
I emphasize that:
. . . bring about the orderly marketing of staple commodities at prices fair to the producer and consumer alike.
The remaining two paragraphs have no relevance to the matter I am discussing, so I shall not read them. I admit that when I see a great Liberal newspaper like the Winnipeg Free Press finding some difficulty in approving this agreement, knowing its devoted attitude toward true Liberal principles I find myself somewhat concerned, and I would cite this agreement of the nations of the world, meeting in international conference, to that newspaper for consideration.
I submit the decision of that conference was that one of the primary purposes of the nations of the world should be agreement to bring about the orderly marketing of staple 
commodities such as wheat, beef, mutton, cotton, wool and other commodities at prices fair to the producer and consumer alike. In other words, Mr. Chairman, there is a spirit abroad in the world to-day, a feeling of live and let live; that if you want to prosper you must let your neighbour prosper; that if the manufacturer is to prosper he must let the farmer prosper as well, in order that the farmer in turn may provide a market for his manufactured products. If Britain is to prosper in her exports of manufactured goods, she must let New Zealand, the countries of South America, Canada and the other primary producing countries prosper in order that they in turn, with a high standard of living, may make use of her manufactured products; and that applies equally to the other manufacturing nations of the world.
I submit that is the basic idea behind this agreement. It is not a bilateral agreement in the old accepted meaning of the term. A bilateral agreement used to mean that if you took from one nation $100,000,000 worth of goods, that nation in turn would take from you $100,000,000 worth of specified goods. That tended to channel the trade of the world between two countries. There is nothing like that about this agreement. This is simply an out-and-out agreement on the part of Great Britain to take so much wheat each year for a period of four years, that there shall be a price of $1.55 for the first two years of the agreement and that for the following two years there shall be a minimum price, but that the actual price shall be negotiated having in mind the relationship which $1.55 had to actual world prices at the time it was being paid. If the English ' language means anything, that means that : if the world price during the first two years of this agreement is higher than $1.55, the British, who are people of their word, will agree to give us a fair price above the world : level during the last two years of the agree- j. ment. Was that not the basic idea behind the establishment of the great wheat pools of western Canada? At that time the idea was that the pools would take the wheat and get the best average price for the year, and then distribute that price to the farmers. In other words the feeling was that in the fall, when the farmer marketed a great deal of his grain, there was a tendency for the price to fall and that after he had sold his grain there was a tendency for the price to rise.
So it was felt that if one organization took the grain, then the farmer could get the average of the prices throughout the year, and he would not have to worry about trying to sell his grain at the highest price.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
This, Mr. Chairman, is just an extension of that idea. This is an attempt to bring about stability, not for just one year at a time but for five years at a time. It was argued this morning, and perhaps well argued, that we might get a higher price for wheat this year and that therefore we should try to get that higher price and not worry about the future, because after all what is the use of worrying about the future since you cannot be sure about it? Well, that is a policy of negation and defeatism. It is a belief that we cannot do better in the future than we have done in the past. This agreement is a venture of faith that, by international agreement, we can do better in the future than we did in the past; that we can introduce an element of stability in regard to the position of primary producers throughout the world, including our own. It introduces the idea that if we can make the primary producers prosperous, then the working people also will be prosperous. Surely all the experiences and hopes of the past are not now to be laughed away and frustrated by saying we must go back to the old ideas of the past, based on the belief that we cannot do any better.
As I said, this agreement is a venture of faith that we can go forward to greater stability, greater fairness to the primary producer. And it is not an exclusive agreement. If there should be any possibility of an international agreement, the very last clause of this document makes provision for the modification of this agreement in accordance therewith. All it means is that we have established one more foundation-stone of stability for the next four or five years-in regard to wheat.
Upon that example, Mr. Chairman, let me express the hope that other primary producing countries will make similar deals with other consuming countries which will provide reasonable prices and reasonable stability in respect of primary products; that upon this basis we may establish stability and a high standard of living for primary producers the world over so that in turn we may also establish a high standard of living for the workers throughout the wTorld. On this basis also we may put to work our tremendous producing power and raise the standard of living of the people throughout the world, and thus do away with the hatreds, the jealousies, the attempts of one country to profit unduly at the expense of another, which helped bring about the last war. This agreement, I think, is just one step along the path mankind must follow toward
the goal of living and letting live, agreeing together and trying to help one another, and for that reason I support it.

I should like to say a few words in connection with this matter, because for many years in this house I have advocated a proper system of protection for the grain growing industry of this country. Everyone wants to see the farmers on the prairies get a proper price for their wheat. I should like to refer briefly to what I said on this subject in the past. To-day we are facing a very acut6 situation with regard to this industry. Years ago my friends of the Liberal Progressives, as they were then, now the Liberal party, believed that this was an all-American industry, or a north and south industry, and not Canada's greatest imperial industry. Let me refer to what I said in this house on May 5, 1924. That is a long time ago, but at that time the farmers of the west had given their support to a party that believed in free trade as far as this industry was concerned, whereas in fact it is the most imperialist industry we have in Canada in dealing with our best customer. As I have said, I want to see them get the best price they can, but do not forget that in 1938 I proposed that a system of underground grain storage reservoirs should be built in Britain, so that when I saw the war sure to come we would have most of our exportable surplus over there. I also wanted to get for our farmers the highest price given for our hard wheat and prevent its being bootlegged with America's course grain, and as a result our gro'wers would get the highest price in the world.
What happened? The hon. gentleman who preceded me came into the house a few years ago. He was a great advocate of free trade on the prairies. If the. people of Saskatchewan want to do something now for the grain industry, let them give fifty per cent free of the 200,000 bushels of wheat Britain must have to-day as an appreciation of Britain as our best customer. Let them give it to Britain, so that bread rationing there will not be necessary. The Minister of Agriculture is about to go over to the old country, and when he goes there I hope he will forget all about this business of free trade, which never did anything for the man who grows the crops on the prairies, the dirt farmer as he was called by the Drury government in the old days. This is what I said back in 1924:
The best friend of the western wheat grower is the policy of protection, as that policy has been and should be extended and administered by the founders and soldiers of the national policy, the Conservative party of Canada. The
Supply-Trade and Commerce

western wheat grower has eaten the sour grapes of free trade. No wonder the western wheat growers' teeth are set on edge. The weste'rn wheat grower has taught himself to believe, or has allowed so-called leaders to persuade him, that wheat growing in western Canada is a continental industry, an industry that must prosper by reason of the admission of the product to the United States market or perish because of its exclusion. I submit that wheat growing in -western Canada is the most truly national, the most widely imperial of all Canada's great industries. The markets of the British Empire mean more and the markets of the American section of the North American continent mean less to the wheat growers of Canada than to any other class of Canadian producers. ...
Progressive Liberals or Liberal Progressives profess that they are the best friends of the western wheat grower. They insist that their quack medicine of free trade is a sure cure-all for all the ailments of the western provinces.
I went on to say:
Ontario has not yet recovered from four years of free trade preaching and blue ruin prophecy. . . . Ontario sent the Ontario end of the Progressive party about its business. Ontario has learned that a few months will not suffice to bring back the business opportunities that were driven away. . . .
Then I continued, May 5, 1924:
I wish now to deal with the wheat growing industry showing that its future depends on adequate protection, that it is not a continental but the most imperial of all our industries, and that protection is the best friend of the wheat grower, and the day will come when he will see it . . .
I believe in free trade only to the extent, I repeat, that if I had sat in the last parliament I would have tried to prove myself a free trader, -when the hon. member from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) without protest or let or hindrance from the Progressives and the other sort of Liberals, proved himself a protectionist . . .
But the Union government honestly tried to protect the western wheat producer against the big interests. The western wheat producers have fulfilled in their experience with the hon. member for Marquette and his followers in this house the words of scripture. "A man's foes shall be they of his household." _ The worst enemy of the western wheat growers is the policy of the Progressive party, its leaders and its representatives in this house.
Later I went on to say:
I plead for a departure from this free trade law of supply and demand and acceptance of the principles of the old national policy in our dealings with all provinces from Yukon to Prince Edward Island.
That national policy would benefit farmers and industrial workers alike. The industrial workers are the forgotten men by this house in 1946, and an industrial relations committee has been meeting here for weeks to give them the protection to-day for which I pleaded in those days. I went on to say:
I plead for a departure from the free trade law of supply and demand and an application of the principles_ of the old national policy to other industries in this country from the manu-

facturing of agricultural implements up to wheat growing. Leave the wheat growing industry of the west to the workings of the law of supply and demand and that law would not fill the west with wheat growers. If that law did fill the west with wheat growers, wheat would not be worth 50 cents a bushel.
And not long after that it went down to 38 cents a bushel.
The free trade law of supply and demand now costs the wheat grower of the west $25,000,000 per annum. I am advised, and believe, that free trade conditions supported by those free trade organizations, the grain exchanges, keep $25,000,000 per annum out of the pockets of Canadians who raise high quality wheat, and put that $25,000,000 per annum into the pockets of the native and alien exploiters who handle high grade Canadian wheat. The Progressive and non-Progressive sections of the Liberal party support grain exchanges and oppose grain inquiries. That party or those parties would sooner talk about agricultural implements than to try to protect the wheat growers pf the west by a departure from free trade conditions. The only cure for these free trade conditions is a return to the ideals of the national policy, the application of the principles of protection. Free trade conditions have failed to maintain the identity of Canada's high grade wheat from the point of production to the ultimate market for that wheat.
At that time the Prime Minister rose in this house and announced the appointment of a royal commission headed by Chief Justice Turgeon. I need not read the report of that commission; it speaks for itself, but it will be found that all the statements I made at that time with regard to the bootlegging of course grains on the Atlantic seaboard in America were founded upon fact.
That great imperial newspaper the Toronto Telegram spent a lot of money in telling the people of the prairie provinces and the people of Ontario that this was really a national industry, that instead of being a north and south industry it was an east and west industry over to Great Britain and our allies and the markets of the world. What has been the result? From the time that commission was appointed they have set up eight or nine or ten different forms of protection during the past eight years or more, and the chickens are coming home to roost.
In conclusion I want to say that I hope that this matter has not been forgotten. Four or five days have been devoted to this but not one day has been devoted to the protection of the industrial worker. The only government that did anything for the white-collared people and the industrial workers was the Bennett government which set up the price spreads inquiry in 1933, 1934 and 1935. We are here to-day to fix the price of wheat and grant all kinds of protection to it in prices, although the actual price is set by world conditions.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Efforts should be made to hold our best customer, Great Britain. When the government saw the war coming in 1936, 1937 and 1938 they should have taken some action and little has been done since then. Hon. members will recall the time when a man with 400 acres was given an acreage bonus not to sow 200 acres. There were all forms of protection. I had a list of them in a return but I shall not read it.
The people of the prairies were responsible for the condition of the grain growing industry in the past; they are responsible for its condition. at the present time, and they will be responsible for its future condition if they do not hold on to their best customer along the lines I have indicated, the mother country. We have had a great number of grain inquiries. Instead of taking up four or five days of the time of the house toward the end of the session, I think this was really a function earlier in the session for the agriculture committee. That is a splendid committee. We have many able men in the house from farming communities. I plead with hon. members to do something to restore public confidence in our best customers in the old land, Great Britain, France and our allies in the last two wars. This can be done by adopting reasonable protection for this great industry.

WThen speaking on this matter yesterday afternoon I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether any commission was paid to brokers or commission merchants, and this morning he made a reply which to me was not very satisfactory. The minister stated that some commission was paid by the purchaser but that it did not affect the farmer directly or indirectly. In my opinion that is not quite correct because I think you will find the purchasers will reduce the price they pay by the amount of commission paid to the brokers.
At the present time 160 million bushels of our wheat are being sold to the British government for the next two years, and 140 million bushels for the succeeding two years. There is no excuse in the world for keeping the commission merchants in Winnipeg or anywhere else on the dole by paying commissions on these deals. This is a deal between departments of governments or 'boards set up by governments in two different countries. I can see no reason for subsidizing these fellows as has been done in the past at the expense of the grain growers.

Does he pay anything to the Winnipeg men?

I do not think the farmers of this country should be penalized any longer. As hon. members know, on previous occasions I have introduced bills to close the grain exchange altogether. The bill that I introduced this session was sent to the agriculture committee, but because a number of other committees were sitting it was not possible to have the bill dealt with this year. I gave notice that if the bill was not dealt with this year I would introduce it next session, and that is still my intention.
I am not particularly concerned with the percentage of commission that is paid on these deals, but I am concerned' over the grain exchange being allowed to operate. The way prices have fluctuated in the past has meant that the farmers were robbed, and I feel satisfied that the same thing will happen in the future. As an illustration I should like to refer to what has happened in connection with rye. On July 30 the price of cash rye in Winnipeg was $3.04 per bushel, but by August 10 the price hadi dropped down to $1,894 cents per bushel.
That is just when the farmer is selling his grain.

As the hon. member for Selkirk says, that is when the farmer is selling his grain, That is a drop of approximately 38 per cent. The farmer is robbed of that difference in price, but of course the fellows on the grain exchange make their commissions regardless of the price at which it is soldi. I think it is a crime; it is just a steal from the farmers. If there are any representatives in the house of the grain exchange or the northwest millers association I should like them to convey that message to those organizations. Until this legalized steal is stopped I intend to continue to introduce bills to close the grain exchange in order to make these members get out and go to work.

I should like to ask the minister a question along the lines of that asked by the hon. member who has just spoken. We have a crop in prospect this year of anywhere from 450 to 500 million bushels of wheat. We are providing for a sale of 160 million bushels to Great Britain. If we allow 90 million bushels for home consumption, for



Supply-Trade and Commerce
feed, seed and flour, that leaves us with probably 200. million bushels still to be sold to other countries. What is the intention of the government with regard to these sales to other countries? Are they to be made direct to individuals in those countries, or to government agencies, or are the facilities of the Winnipeg grain exchange or any other grain exchange to be used? What is the method that is to be used in disposing of the grain that is not covered by this contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No grain exchange in Winnipeg or anywhere else is going to be used as far as the Canadian government or the wheat board is concerned. I am told that certain buyers in foreign countries are in the habit of buying through shippers or brokers and I do not know to what extent they will continue to do that.
Is that for the duration of the contract, or just for this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: As far as I know it is for the duration of the contract. I can answer the hon. member's question by stating that it is the intention to carry on indefinitely in the way I have just stated.

I understood from the
minister that any exporting firm in this or any other country which makes a deal outside of this contract must place the order with a broker here who will buy direct from the wheat board. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.

This morning the Minister of Agriculture stated that the 12^ per cent in the price of agricultural machinery would be offset through the Canadian dollar being now on a parity with the United States dollar. We all agreed that that should be so, but that is not what is happening, because the last word I had from the west shows that an $1,800 binder is now quoted at over $2,000. Is the government going to take, steps to see that the prices of farm machinery are controlled? It seems to me that since the government allowed that increase of 12J per cent and brought the Canadian dollar on a parity with the United States dollar, the government would be justified in reducing the farm machinery increase from 12J per cent to 2\ per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is a matter of government policy.

But farm machinery is being bought in such large quantities prior to the harvest that the question is important

now; for our farmers are paying these increased prices. If the government is going to act it will have to act quickly.

In regard to quota deliveries during the second, third and fourth years of this contract, will the quota be applied only during a certain portion of the year until the heavy run of wheat comes, or throughout the whole year?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It will be the policy of the wheat board to open up the quotas just as soon as it can.
The farmers will be able to deliver all the wheat they can grow during the life of this contract to July 31, 1950?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is my understanding.
What will be the acreage basis under this agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The present authorized acreage is approximately 22,000,000. The original basis was 65 per cent of the 1940 acreage, but since then adjustments have been made and at the present time the authorized acreage is approximately 22,000,000. We are operating on that basis.

Will new acreage be permitted to come under cultivation? Thousands of veterans are returning to agriculture and getting themselves established on new land. There will have to be some adjustment made to take care of them, and I want that clearly understood.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The wheat board have been doing that right along.

With regard to the five-year participation period, one of the great objections is that the farmer will not be able to realize on his participation certificates beyond 10 cents now and 14 to 16 cents on the 1944 crop until July 31, 1950.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is correct. After payments have been made on the 1943 crop, the 1944 crop and 10 cents on the 1945 crop, and that will take some time, the next participation payments will not be made until the profits of the five-year pool are ascertained.
That will probably be in 1951.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I should think so.

At the very earliest. Is there no way in which the government can make a participation payment at the end of the third year instead of the farmer having to wait five years? That is just a bit too long.

A good many farmers have their money in participation certificates, and with rising costs they are going to be in a difficult position. Some will be compelled to go to the banks and borrow money, because even though they have participation certificates the banks do not take them as collateral. I would strongly urge that a partial payment be made at the end of three years instead of five years. That would greatly relieve the position of the grain growers.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do not see how that could be done, but it is a matter that might well be taken into consideration.

I raised that point this morning. I am not able to understand why the twenty cents which would apply on the next two years' crops should not be paid following the end of those two years. The answer given was it was being held to average up the price for the five-year period. Is there any other object which the wheat board has in mind in holding up payment of the participation certificates for five years?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The plan provides for a five-year pool, and the participation payments covering the five-year pool will be made on the basis of the profits made by the board in the next five years.

I asked another question this morning as to the subsidy on flour for domestic use in Canada. The government has been paying a subsidy of 47 f cents a bushel. I do not suppose that subsidy will be paid on flour exported?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.
How do you adjust the matter between the two lots of flour?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The mills make a report to the wheat board every month. Those reports are audited, so there will be no difficulty about that at all.

One question that bothers me more than anything else is that all manufactured goods are exported on a rising market. Is there anything in mind to bring about parity between farm prices and the prices of the goods the farmer needs in order to produce and for his living?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.

I think we are all agreed that we want stability and that this agreement is a step in that direction. But there is one flaw in it, and I am wondering if this point was discussed with the British representatives when the negotiations were taking place. There is no relationship between the price of 63260-305.1
our wheat being sold to Britain and the prices of the goods which Britain has to sell to us. We are buying certain of these articles and it seems to me there should be some relationship between the price of wheat we are selling to Britain and the prices of the goods she is selling to us. I know that in negotiating agreements with other parts of the commonwealth that factor was taken into consideration. Was it discussed in the negotiations with the British people in connection with this agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: There was no discussion of that, and I really do not see how there could be any hope of arriving at agreement on it.

In the agreement which Britain reached with New Zealand the matter was discussed and adjustments were made in the agreement to cover that point. I know it is much easier to do that in the case of New Zealand because she buys a lot of goods direct from Britain which we do not. But if this wheat agreement is to be fair to the farmers there must be some relationship between their costs and the prices of what they have to buy. I know it is very difficult for a government which does not believe in planning except from day to day to do that. Nevertheless I am still of the opinion that that is the only permanent solution of our problem, and I was wondering if the government had been farsighted enough to discuss that aspect of the matter with Britain when negotiating this agreement.

(The agreement follows):
The government of Canada and the government of the United Kingdom, recognizing that their mutual interest in the maintenance of reasonable prices and adequate supplies of wheat for consumers and of steady and remunerative prices for producers can best be met by international cooperation in the expansion of world trade and employment, have entered into the following arrangements designed to ensure a measure of security in the supply and of stability in the price of wheat supplied by Canada to the United Kingdom:
1.	(a) The United Kingdom government undertakes to purchase and the Canadian government undertakes to sell the following quantities of Canadian wheat, which quantities include wheat to be processed into flour for sale to the United Kingdom government:
(i)	within the crop year 1946-47, 160.000,000 bushels;
(ii)	within the crop year 1947-48, 160,000,000 bushels;
(iii)	within the crop eyar 1948-49, 140,000,000 bushels;
(iv)	within the crop year 1949-50, 140,000,000 bushels;
A bushel shall be of the weight of 60 pounds avoirdupois.

(b)	In the event of the United Kingdom requiring from Canada any additional quantities of wheat that the Canadian government is prepared to make available, such additional quantities which the Canadian government offers and the United Kingdom government accepts shall in all respects be subject to the provisions of this agreement.
(c)	Of the total quantity of wheat specified above for each crop year, the United Kingdom government agrees to take the following quantity in long tons in the form of flour:
1946-	47-500,000 tons as a minimum, with an additional quantity not exceeding 140,000 tons to be determined by negotiations in the lighj of the out-turn of the crop.
1947-	48-400,000 tons as a minimum, with an additional quantity not exceeding 140,000 tons to be determined by negotiations in the light of the out-turn of the crop.
1948-	49-300,000 tons as a minimum, the actual tonnage to be negotiated by the 1st July, 1947.
1949-	50-300,000 tons as a minimum, the actual tonnage to be negotiated by the 1st July, 1948.
(d)	The rate and place of deliveries of wheat and flour shall be determined from time to time by mutual agreement.
2.	(a) The price per bushel to be paid by the United Kingdom government to the Canadian government on the basis number one Manitoba northern, in store Fort William/Port Arthur, Vancouver or Churchill, shall be as follows:
(i)	In respect of wheat bought and sold in the crop year 1946-47, $1.55.
(ii)	In respect of wheat bought and sold in the crop year 1947-48, $1.55.
(iii)	In respect of wheat bought and sold in the crop year 1948-49, not less than $1.25.
(iv)	In respect of wheat bought and sold in the crop year 1949-50, not less than $1.
(b)	The actual prices to be paid for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year 1948-49 shall be negotiated and settled between the United Kingdom government and the Canadian government not later than the 31st December. 1947. and prices for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year 1949-50 shall be negotiated and settled not later than the 31st December, 1948. In determining the prices for these two crop years, 1948-49 and 1949-50, the United Kingdom government will have regard to any difference between the prices paid under this agreement in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years and the world prices for wheat in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years.
(c)	The prices to be paid for grades other than number one Manitoba northern to be delivered under this agreement shall be determined yearly in consultation between the United Kingdom government and the Canadian government.
(d)	In addition to the prices detailed in Section (a) of this article, the United Kingdom government undertakes to pay such carrying and forwarding charges as may be mutually arranged.
(e)	Payment shall be made in full in Canadian funds at par Winnipeg by the United Kingdom payments office against presentation of completed statements of claim or otherwise as may be mutually agreed.
3.	It is agreed that the United Kingdom government may sell or dispose of the wheat and flour purchased under this agreement in

Supply-Trade and Commerce
whatsoever manner the United Kingdom government may deem expedient both in regard to destination and price.
4.	(a) The Canadian government will use its best endeavours to arrange that the qualities of wheat set out in article 1 (a) shall at all times be available and at the disposal of the United Kingdom government within the stipulated dates and in accordance with the rates and places of delivery determined under section (d) of article 1 of this agreement.
(b) The United Kingdom government will use its best endeavours to arrange for the provision of the required ocean tonnage within the stipulated dates and in accordance with the rates and places of delivery determined under section (d) of article 1 of this agreement.
5.	It is agreed that the detailed terms and conditions relating to such matters as carrying and forwarding charges, grades, routing of shipments and all other matters incidental to the fulfilment of this agreement shall be discussed and settled from time to time and incorporated in documents to form annexures to this agreement.
6.	It is mutually understood that matters arising from, or incidental to, the operation of this agreement may at the instance of either party become subjects of discussion between the parties to this agreement.
7.	Having in mind the general purposes which this agreement is designed to serve, the two governments have agreed that its terms and conditions shall be subject to any modification or amendment which may be necessary to bring it into conformity with any international agreements or arrangements hereafter entered into to which both governments are parties.
Done in duplicate, in Ottawa, on the twenty-fourth day of July, 1946.
For the Government of Canada:
Jas. A. MacKinnon.
For the Government of the United Kingdom: P. A. Clutterbuck.
I have no intention of venturing into the details of this agreement; I should be just a sheep in the midst of wolves and, probably, be torn from all sides. But I do want to make some observations-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, oh.

I assure the Minister of Veterans Affairs that they will be brief. They have to do with some remarks which were made this morning by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. The hon. member, in hailing this agreement, correctly described it as a great step forward to a controlled economy, and I heard no sign of any demur from the opposite side of the house, so that I am going to take it upon myself to say one or two things about it.
I have noticed that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar takes his cue from the Apostle Paul, in that he tries to be "all things to all men." It is not long ago since I had occasion to quote him in this house to the
following effect: "We are not opposed to private enterprise, but we demand that private enterprise should take the risks if it takes the rewards." I said I could agree with that. I can only assume that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar uttered' those remarks after having associated with some people engaged in private enterprise, whom he found to be, like himself, quite civilized, and therefore he had difficulty in regarding them as members of "the jungle"-to quote a phrase socialists sometimes use. But this morning, I assume after returning from the meeting of the other apostles in the west, he showed a feeling of enthusiasm about socialism, and it seemed1 to me that he went a very long way. It is true that he referred to laissez-faire, which I recognize is an extreme form of private enterprise, and a form of private enterprise which has to be curtailed in various ways. Nevertheless he got into a pretty full flood of socialist feeling, as I understood him, when he described this agreement as being the precursor of other agreements, and it seemed to me that before it was through he had floated us well out on the sea of socialism, which I do not think all of us wish to embark on.
It is true-and for this I give him credit- that when he spoke about a controlled economy he said there would be no regimentation. That is something which puzzles me very much. Apparently those who believe in these views think you can have a control which is not a control; it is going to be all very nice; nobody is going to tell anybody else what he must do; everything will be by persuasion.
Does the hon. member for (Muskoka-Ontario believe in the kind of private enterprise which Mr. Gladstone Murray speaks of as responsible enterprise?

If I understand what Mr. Gladstone Murray has said, as quoted by the hon. member, certainly I mean that. I would go farther and say, while I am on the point, that there must be regulation, and in some cases more regulation than others. But I come back to this point of control and regimentation, because I think it is an important point.
People must try to be realistic about this. To me it is inevitable that regimentation, however pleasant you try to make it, will still be regimentation, and it will still involve a few people giving other people orders. I once read an essay on murder, in which it was apparently argued that even murder could be done in a pleasant way. The essayist remarked, "I once knew a bulldog which murdered another bulldog with pleasing circumstances of
Supply-Trade and Commerce

good taste." I am prepared to believe that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, who, though I disagree with him, I must say always seems to be very agreeable, might try to make control and even regimentation as palatable as possible, just as the pleasant bulldog did.
But why I really rose in my place was this. I think, regardless of our views and differences, all of us would* like to feel that we are realistic. Frankly, I think members of the C.C.F. are often not realistic, and especially they are in grave danger of constantly ignoring the fact that this country is one which lives or dies by export trade. That being so

and this is really my excuse for being on my feet at all 

I wish to draw attention to a short extract from the London Economist, dealing with the position of England and with the task facing the British government, the task especially of finding the export trade by which, as the Economist in effect points out, they either live or die. If their export trade is good they 'will live, and if it is not they will die, or at any rate suffer a grievous reduction of their standard of living.
What about imports?
I always try to couple imports and exports.
We are not in England; we are in Canada.

I should like to invite your attention to this quotation, because it is right on the target. I do not think any intelligent man can listen to this without asking himself whether it is true or false, and if it is true, it has searching and far-reaching implications for us. The article, which appears in the issue of July 27, at page 82, begins:
This is a strange task-
The task is that of finding sufficient export trade to enable them to prosper.
This is a strange task for a socialist government to find itself embarking upon. For competition in the world market still has those ugly features that socialists strive to banish from the domestic scene. The foreign purchaser is rarely amenable to "control." The foreign competitor does not submit to "coordination." "Fixed prices" are a rare exception and "orderly marketing" still rarer. Subsidies, the last resort in the domestic field of a government that cannot otherwise make an industry's ends meet, are regarded in the foreign field as almost equivalent to a declaration of war. The foreign customer is obstinate about buying where he can buy cheapest. Price, in fact, is the very essence of exporting. Quality, of course, plays its part; but quality alone, without a competitive price, will be useless.
Wherever else the labour government may be able to escape from the operations of the law of supply and demand-that law of the jungle 
that socialist orators are so fond of denouncing -they will have to face it in export markets. However much they may succeed in the domestic market, in substituting the welfare of the producer for the service of the consumer as the test of economic efficiency, they cannot do so in exports. . .
They will not find it easy to be coordinators at home and competitors abroad. They will need to be very stern in letting not their right hand know what their left hand doeth. Their chosen right hand is Sir Stafford Cripps; but he has not been able to prevent a little left-handedness creeping into his activities, as when, by some sort of conditioned reflex,-
I do not know exactly what "conditional reflex" means.
-he nationalized the Liverpool cotton market. That sort of instinct will have to be sternly repressed if the government are to perform as well in the role of Doctor Jekyll as in that of Mr. Hyde. They have just about three years-
The reason for the reference to three years is that they reckon that will be the time when the American and) Canadian credits will run out.
They have just about three years to prove that their economic policy can meet the brutal test of economic efficiency-that is, whether or not it can produce better goods, at lower prices than other countries. If it can, the world will be at its feet. If it cannot, no amount of appeal to social justice, no "planning" or schemes of social security will save the country from a sharp reduction in its standard of living.
Whether hon. members agree with that statement or not, I believe everyone will agree that it is at least a clear statement of a certain view which I suggest is realism. I am sorry the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is not here at the moment. I suggest that these words apply to this country just as precisely as they do to Great Britain.
'Mr. COTE (Matapedia-Matane): I would fully agree with the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) if he were sitting in the House of Commons in England. I should like to see him there some day. His great associate, Mr. Bennett, sits in the House of Lords. From the point of view of the British government, there is no doubt whatever that the article from which he has quoted and the argument which he is promoting are right. But unfortunately for the hon. member, we are not in Westminster. We are in the House of Commons of Canada, in Ottawa.
What has that to do with it?
Wait a minute. You will find out.
Not from you.

You will be surprised, and disappointed. I am not going to say that I am an expert on this ques-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
tion. Far from it. The hon. member for Miuskoka-Ontario knows me better than to suppose that I would pose an as expert, but I hope that I shall be understood by members of all parties when I make the statement I am about to make. When we have to discuss any matter here, why should we introduce into this house the views and the concepts of people with whom we are trading? Exports from England to this country are imports as far as Canada is concerned, and exports from the Canadian soil to England are imports to the English. It is not one and the same problem at all. I suggest that it is about time that we in this House of Commons tried to understand the problem as it really is.
We have given 81,250,000,000 to England, and we have done so after many other grants; and I voted upon it with the greatest satisfaction that I have ever had in my life. Why? I will tell you why. I felt like a man paying the last instalment on a promissory note to the bank, a payment from a debtor who was becoming a creditor. I contend, therefore, that we should deal with this problem now before us as we deal with all problems as between exporters and importers-Canada-United Kingdom-on the basis that we are a nation and that we must analyse the situation instead of taking advice either from Westminster or from hon. members on the other side for whom I have every respect.

Has there been any recent change in the wheat board's policy in granting permits to a number of brothers farming together, or to father and son? Last year I received several complaints from organizations in my constituency to the effect that the wheat board was attempting to get brothers to sell wheat under one permit instead of, as before, under two or three. The same thing was complained of with regard to father and son. These people fear that if this were carried out they would be told that under the P.F.A. Act they were one unit instead of two or three and thereby the bonus would be cut down. Moreover, it would cause confusion, because if one brother wanted to sell coarse grains and another brother wanted to buy coarse grains, if they were operating under one permit, a transaction of that sort would not be permitted, whereas under separate permits one might sell and the other buy. I cannot understand why, as in the past, brothers should not be allowed to sell under separate permits.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The chairman of the wheat board tells me that without knowing more of the circumstances it would be impossible to give an answer.

Has there been any definite change in policy, or was this a case of
individual action to meet certain particular cases where they thought a mistake was being made?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am advised that there is no definite change in policy.

I was intrigued by the reference of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario to the wolves and sheep, and I confess that by the time he was through I felt it difficult to distinguish between the wolves and the sheep.
Mr. MACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontano;: I was the sheep.

What I wish to refer to is the argument that he tried to develop-or so it struck me at any rate-in favour of what might be called unrestricted or uncontrolled trading as opposed to the direct method. I must say at the outset that for my own part I would prefer to have seen a multilateral rather than a bilateral agreement, because that is the direction in which we are attempting to go in these days. On the other hand, I would rather see a bilateral agreement than none at all. I do not need to go into the reasons for that because it has been covered.
I am not altogether happy or contented with' the terms of the contract because I feel, as I have said before, that the initial price for wheat could have been higher than the price we have obtained. I have a simple calculation here which shows how I make that contention. For example, the initial price was $1.25, with participation certificates of twelve cents on the 1943 crop, making a total of $1.37. If we were to take the pattern set by the government itself in connection with increasing prices, for example the 12J per cent increase on farm implements-and that seems to be the pattern right along for manufactured articles-and added 12J per cent to the $1.37, or eighteen cents, we would bring the price up to $1.55. I think the government could have been bold enough to take that step and to have guaranteed a price of $1.55 for four years, instead of for two years.
On the other hand, however, I cannot bring myself to agree with those ideas which have been expressed by hon. members to my right, and for this reason. I have listened carefully in the last two days to speeches made by hon. members in the Progressive Conservative party, and I have failed thus far in my own mind to crystallize anything in the form of an alternative to this agreement. We have heard considerable by way of denunciation of it, and some of the criticism was good. But
Supply-Trade and Commerce

I have not heard anything which could be put in the place of this agreement which would merit my support.
The only indication we have had along that line was what we heard to-day, and that amounted to going back to the principle of laissez-faire which was so roundly condemned by the hon. member himself. The process of accusing the leader of this group of welcoming the agreement because it means regimentation, giving orders, and all those terrible things which are supposed to be tied to controls, I cannot accept, because it is not so. We must definitely make up our minds that this is true, as long as we live, in any society, because we have reached the point where somebody is going to do the controlling. The only choice I can see is as to whether we shall have control, in which we as a parliament can participate, or whether we shall have control of our prices from the outside.
Apparently the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario prefers control by people from the outside. Evidently he would think that if we were to have nothing to do with the setting of prices here, everybody would be happy. The result would be that somebody would set the price for us; somebody would set this mythical world price. It might be some monopoly or trust company or bank over which we have no control. I object to that type of control. If we are to have the control or regimentation which is necessary, then let us have such control emanate from a public body which can be controlled in turn by the voters of this country. Then we shall have a say in how much control there will be and in which respects we shall have it. If we do not do that we shall have to accept controls which are imposed upon us by private enterprise, for its own benefit.

I should like to say a few words in reply to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, who made reference to the leader of this party and to his hailing of this agreement. I heard clearly what my leader said, and I noticed he said that whereas this agreement gave stability, and whereas it gave for a period of years some security to the farmer, he hailed it as a step in the right direction.
Apparently the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario is very much afraid that we are leading to regimentation, and that such regimentation will not be to his liking. I think the rank and file of people in Canada who are going to benefit from such control as this will hail this contract. The people who will squeal about it are those who previously operated the grain exchange and the stock exchange, those who speculated to their own advantage

and to the detriment of others. We shall have squealing from the monopolies who, to their own advantage, have the power to withhold necessities from the rank and file of the people. So far as I am concerned, and so far as the rank and file of the people in this country are concerned, we are not going to worry about that regimentation, even if it means the elimination of those people who maintain their rackets in that particular field.
Then, the hon. member seemed somewhat concerned about what the ultimate result would be when we approach the international field. When nations throughout the world carry on an exchange of agreements on this basis, through a process of governments arranging with governments rather than with exchanges and people on world exchanges, or with world monopolies, it is to the advantage of the rank and file and for the benefit of people everywhere, rather than for the benefit of just a few who may be in control in the international field. Under this process we have regimentation in the right place, and I do not think the rank and file of people will object to it.
I listened with a good deal of attention, as I usually do, when the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario speaks.
Then I wonder why you do not agree with me.
He did admit that we must have some regulation.
I always have.

He also says that we must be realistic. I would say to him that I remember only too well that period following the first great war when there was a reopening of trading in wheat on the Winnipeg grain exchange, and when we had an example of people trying to operate the economy of our country along the lines which apparently the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario is advocating: "Be sure you do not have any regimentation. Be sure your regulations will not hurt those who want to go ahead with their system of laissez-faire"-of which the hon. member himself seems now to be somewhat dubious.
There are thousands upon thousands of farmers in western Canada who remember, most realistically, the period of time in the thirties, when the government in power had much the same conception about how the affairs of the country should be run as does the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, when we had the privilege of producing some of the finest wheat we ever produced in our

Supply-Veterans Affairs
lives, the very best of No. 1 hard. You know, Mr. Chairman, I am so realistic that I remember only too well the days when I hauled that wheat to the elevators and got thirty-eight cents a bushel for it.

Was it worth any
more than that in any other country of the world at that time?

I would add that there
were regulations then. There was regimentation, not regimentation by government, but regimentation by those who controlled the marketing of grain in our country. When we talk about regimentation we must remember that very often there is regimentation and control exercised by people who are not acting on behalf of the people generally, but rather on behalf of a small group.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

Could the hon. member have obtained any more for a bushel of wheat in any other nation during the thirties than he got in Canada at that time-from any government, including the socialist governments of that time?

I am not excusing the
successors of the union government any more than I am excusing others. Had the governments of those days had the vision and foresight following the first great war to have consummated agreements similar to this one, in all probability we would not have had the condition later on which was referred to by the hon. member for Souris.
I should like to say a few words about this agreement. The leader of this group has spoken, as well as other hon. members in the group. I believe-and I am convinced that this goes for many farmers throughout Canada -that while in this agreement there may be certain provisions which are not entirely to our satisfaction, and while there may be some things-some of which have been mentioned- we should like to have improved, by and large the farmers of this country, and especially those who would come under the operations of this policy announced by the government, are going to accept it as a step in the right direction. They are doing that because they consider that, despite its shortcomings, there is much good in it.

I am not going to make a lengthy speech, but rise simply to ask a question of the minister.
I would say first of all, however, that I should like to draw one inconsistency to the 63260-306
attention of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario. The hon. member is always so good1-natured, polite and courteous that I know he will not object to my drawing this to his attention. He read from an article in the London Economist, I believe he said it was, and during the course of his reading he came to a point where he made the observation, "I do not quite understand that, myself." But he indicated in his remarks that he agreed with the article, even though there were some parts in it he did not quite understand.
I have a question which I have asked before, but perhaps I did not ask it clearly enough to get the answer I had expected. Therefore it was my own fault that I did not get the right answer. My question is this. The wheat board is going to accept delivery of all wheat for the next four years. It will deliver approximately 160 million bushels this year direct to Britain, according to contract. There will be other amounts left over for outside markets, wherever they may be found. Does the wheat board intend to offer for sale on the pit of the Winnipeg grain exchange the wheat which is not covered by the contract with Great Britain?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
