speechtext: H4. Departmental administration, $1,554,712.

It is refreshing to get away from all this talk about wheat and chaff we

Supply-Veterans Affairs

have been smothered in for the last three or four days. Coming from the maritime provinces, I find myself in somewhat the same position as the hon. member for Durham, in wondering if there is any other part of Canada except the three prairie provinces.
I believe it has been the practice to permit a general debate when the first item of each department is called. I do not intend to take up much time this afternoon, nor do I fell I would be justified in doing so. Veterans affairs have been discussed not only in the house when the bills respecting veterans were before it but, as every hon. member knows, for weeks and weeks in the veterans affairs committee. I do not think much more could be said either here or anywhere else on the subject. Any attempt at a lengthy discussion must result in repetition. At this stage of the session I would not feel justified in proceeding at length, and I am sure most other hon. members would feel the same way.
However, there is one point I believe I should emphasize, and it is this, that if there should be any lack of criticism in these estimates at the present time it arises from the fact that the subject matter has been discussed on other occasions, and such lack of discussion must not be considered by the government as an indication of entire satisfaction with the results obtained thus far. Many hon. member know that we pressed for things in committee meetings which we did not get. It would take too long this afternoon to mention them in detail.
However, I might say that the Veterans' Land Act has come in for a considerable amount of criticism. Many settlers feel they are not getting what they should get. There is criticism in connection with small holdings, and the building of houses under the Veterans' Land1 Act.
Then the matter of imperials was discussed, and many hon. members expressed the view that the imperials were not justly treated. Mention has been made of the fire fighters- and I bring these matters to the attention of the committee only to show that, while there may not be extensive criticism of the minister's estimates there are still many things which could and have been criticized in the past.
I have noticed1 that on occasions hon. members bring to the house letters which they have received from constitutents setting out certain points of criticism. I am satisfied, from the number I have received, that if all hon. members were to bring their personal letters to the house and proceed to read them, practically nothing else would be done.

We have been told by the minister, and to a great extent we agree, that the legislation put through the house has been good. I think he said it was the best to be found in any country in the world. While we do not all agree on that-I have no doubt the United States consider they have some of the best veterans legislation in the world'-we do agree that our legislation is good-. There can be no doubt about that. As I said a few da3-s ago, there is no reason why Canada should not have good legislation for its veterans, because I do not believe there is any country in the world better fitted than this Canada to look after its veterans.
When one stops to consider the situation in other countries he recalls that most of the countries in Europe were overrun by war and suffered far more than we did. Their cities, towns and public utilities were destroyed and ravaged, and the people are bankrupt. So that I say Canada is in a 'better position to look after her veterans than is almost any other country. While we may claim great credit for it, and while we may be entitled to credit, yet it would be veiy much to our discredit if it were not true.
The most serious criticism being made in Canada to-day in connection with veterans affairs is not with the legislation which was dealt with by the veterans affairs committee, and which has been passed in the form of bills, as with the administration. As has been mentioned time after time in this house, the two matters which concern the veterans most to-day are jobs and housing. I know these come under other departments, but they are the two great problems for the veteran. They must be solved by the government and by this country if our veterans are to be properly rehabilitated and receive what we consider is their due for the suffering they have undergone and the sacrifice they made for this country and for civilization.
We have passed many acts. As I said a few moments ago, they are good acts, but the best intentions in the world as far as those acts are concerned will be frustrated unless they are properly administered. The passing of an act is sometimes quite a simple matter, but it is an entirely different matter to carry out the terms of an act. I have pointed out before, and I think it will bear repeating, that at the head of these different departments of the veterans affairs are men who are capable, but there has been some reason for complaint in connection with the men to be found across the country. I suppose- that is owing to the fact that the department cannot always get

Supply-Veterans Affairs
the best men. Sometimes, if these men are not properly checked they do not take the interest in their work they should.
That is not only true in this country; it applies to others as well. I have read articles about what happened in the United States after the last war, particularly with reference to hospitalization. After the last war, the public there began to lose interest in the veterans and there was not as good administration as there should have been. I hope that that will not happen to veterans of this war. I trust that these new acts will be so administered that there will be little fault to be found as far as the veterans are concerned.
I think we all recognize the fact that the soldier finished his job when the war ended. He did a splendid job. During the war there were many organizations which rendered assistance in 'hospitals and other service organizations. They did much to help those who were carrying the burden of war. It has been the experience in the past that, when a war is over, people turn to their own duties and responsibilities and leave this other responsibility to the government. They more or less wash their hands of it. I hope that that will not be the case after this war.
There are many large hospitals from one end of the country to the other and there are many service men who will have to remain in those hospitals for years to come. There are many social organizations which could lighten t'heir burden and assist them in many other ways. As I say, I hope that, now that the war is over, these matters will not be left entirely to civil service officials or to the Department of Veterans Affairs, but that these social organizations which did such a splendid work during the war will feel that they still have a responsibility to the soldier who has to spend his time in hospital.
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs): In a word may I thank the hon. member for Royal for the typically cooperative and constructive remarks he has made this afternoon. They only reflect his attitude all through the meetings of the committee on veterans affairs. In regard to the committees he has mentioned, I can assure him that conferences of our local committees are going on all across the country. Their work has been most helpful and constructive and is tremendously appreciated.
I do not think I should detain the committee at present except to answer such questions as may be asked. We had a splendid committee and I should like to pay a tribute to the members before these estimates are through. I happen to have been thirty years in parliament, and never in my life have I 63260-306J
seen a committee so sustained in their devotion to the public service, both in the cause of the veterans and the cause of Canada, as was the veterans affairs committee of this parliament. Whatever may be the vicissitudes of public life in the future, the members of this committee will always have the reward of conscience from a task well done. If I were in charge of giving out awards, I would grant each one the Canada medal.

On behalf of this group, I should like to say a word on this item. It is not my intention to enter into any prolonged debate and I am not even going to repeat the remarks of the hon. member for Royal. I think he has covered fairly well the points on which there might have been any difference of opinion in the committee. While we did not get all the things we wanted, there was cooperation on the part of the government in granting at least part of our requests. I hope that the same cooperation will exist in the future, because there is no doubt that after we come back to another parliament we shall have found that there are inconsistencies in these acts which will need eliminating. I hope that we shall have the same cooperation from the government in connection with listening to those complaints and remedying some of them.
As the hon. member for Royal has said, you can have the best act in the world, but if the administration and the regulations passed under it are not sympathetic the whole act will be spoiled. Taking it as a whole, I think the administration of these veterans acts has been good, but there will occur in different parts of the dominion inconsistencies which we as members will feel we must bring to the attention of the government. I hope that there will not be any heated arguments when we bring up such matters, because we do so knowing that they are just complaints which should be remedied.
There was one matter which I brought to the attention of the minister a short time ago. This had to do with conflict with respect to veterans regulations concerning men getting medical treatment during the first year after discharge, and certain provincial acts, particularly one in Saskatchewan, with respect to automobile accidents. I hope that the minister will have an opportunity to iron out these difficulties. It is the little things that really make a difference between success or failure in the administration of veterans legislation. It is the failure to remedy a thing quickly enough, to let it drag on, that gives the black jye to what might otherwise be good veterans legislation.
Supply-Veterans Affairs

I believe that we have put through reasonably good veterans legislation. As I said before, perhaps it is not as complete as some of us would have liked. If we were responsible for its administration, perhaps we would not go as far as we are prepared to go when we are in opposition. If we are fair we shall admit these things. I urge the department to give sympathetic consideration to the little differences that will occur throughout the country and have them remedied as quickly as possible so that they will not become open sores and cause dissension among our veterans.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I want to thank my hon. friend for his remarks.

On behalf of this group, I want to say that I agree wholeheartedly with the remarks of the two previous speakers. I do not think anything will be gained by repeating what has already been said. I was a member of the committee which sat last year and the greater part of this session. We covered every phase and angle of veterans affairs, so that it would be a sheer waste of time to travel over the same ground again. The point made by the last speaker was a very good one. No doubt, when we get back to our constituencies, we shall find that certain acts are not working out to the best advantage, but I am satisfied that if we bring defects to the attention of the minister he will give our representations every consideration, and that at the next session, if we have found serious trouble with the legislation, the minister will give us every cooperation.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Thank you.
Mr. IiERRIDGE: As a member of the veterans affairs committee I want to support the remarks of the hon. member for Royal, the hon. member for Melfort and the hon. member for Acadia. I do not think there is any necessity at this time, after the long discussions we have had in the veterans affairs committee to deal with these estimates at length. I want to say that I enjoyed working with the other members of the committee and that throughout the whole of our meetings the spirit was excellent. The intention of all the members was to serve the men they were appointed to serve. I am sure that all members of the house, all veterans and the people of the country will watch with great interest the workings of our veterans legislation during the months ahead, and no doubt next session we shall be prepared to make suggestions that experience will justify. I wish to suggest through you, Mr. Chairman, to the minister that it would be of great advantage to members of the house if they could obtain a copy of the consolidated acts relating to veterans.
[Mr. Wright.[

I notice that there are nine district administrators, with salaries ranging from $3,000 to $5,700. Would the minister indicate on what basis these districts are organized? Are they on a provincial basis, or are they military districts, and what is the reason for the wide variation in salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The basis is an approximation in conformity with military districts, but sometimes it has been necessary to form sub-regional districts for purposes of better administration.

447. Treatment services, $13,761,079.

In keeping with the spirit of cooperation displayed this afternoon, it is not my intention to embark on criticism of this item, but I would appreciate it if the minister would give some thought to methods by which treatment in hospitals could be made more readily available to the veterans. I have in mind the Shaughnessy hospital at Vancouver. A common complaint there is that the men are kept lining up for sometimes two or three days, and the men themselves say sometimes weeks, without actually getting to see a doctor. Then an appointment is made for a certain day. The veteran goes to the admitting office and is told to go over there or to sit down here, and he may stay there for some days. The generality of this complaint leads one to the thought that there must be a shortage of staff in these hospitals which gives rise to this condition. I know that in that hospital most if not all of the doctors are veterans, and I am quite certain they would not willingly keep any veteran waiting. It must be a shortage of staff, and when one looks through these items and sees the salaries that are paid to these doctors one finds a possible explanation of the shortage. I think the same condition exists with regard to the nurses in these hospitals. I know that some of these hospitals have had the greatest difficulty in getting doctors and nurses, and some effort was made to solve that problem by seconding medical personnel from the armed forces; but now the medical personnel in the armed forces are trying to get out of the armed forces as fast as they can. Would the minister make some comment on that and say whether the salary position is responsible for the shortage and whether, in that case,

Supply-Veterans Affairs
any increase will be made in the salaries to make service in these hospitals more attractive to the best class of medical personnel.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: About six or nine months ago the remarks of my hon. friend would have been abundantly justified, but since then we have reorganized the whole medical services of the Department of Veterans Affairs under the able and, may I say, brilliant direction of Brigadier Warner. The salaries, of the doctors are being raised. That was one of the problems that we have had for the last twenty-five years, and my hon. friend is quite correct in what he said on that point. The salaries of the doctors who were working for pensions and national health were far too low, but now we have the whole medical fraternity in Canada united with the department. We have the family doctor scheme; we have consultants; we have specialists; and the salaries have been raised to a maximum of $7,200. Formerly it was approximately $4,200. So that the problem which my hon. friend has quite properly mentioned has been met.

In almost every locality
throughout the country there are local doctors to whom the veterans go for treatment, and I have heard complaints that the scale of fees provided for these doctors is altogether too low. Is anything being done to see that these doctors receive fair remuneration for the work they do for the veterans?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. Within the last few weeks the scale of fees of the local or family doctors for home calls, office calls and hospital visits has been revised substantially.
Does this item of treatment services cover the veterans of the first great war?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
When a veteran who suffered from gas in the first great war continues to be sick and requires treatment and medicine, does he have to pay his local doctor for treatment, medicine and so forth?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If he is a pensioner he does not have to pay for treatment. In any event, he may obtain domiciliary care in a departmental institution.

I know one veteran who, from my own observation, is greatly afflicted with a lung condition. He gets a very small pension of $21 or $22 a month, which is wholly inadequate, for he is unable to work except very occasionally, and his whole pension
goes into medicine. Under the new veterans legislation will he be qualified to obtain medicine free?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He is entitled to a hospital allowance at any time when receiving treatment for a pensionable condition.
Is he entitled to free medicine?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He can get treatment and hospital allowances when being treated for a pensionable condition.
Can he get free treatment at home?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No; only in a hospital or in one of our institutions for domiciliary care.
If he stays at home he is not entitled to free medicine?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He can obtain medicine while on out-patient treatment for pensionable condition if he does not want to go into the hospital.
If he went as an outpatient would he get medicine free?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, absolutely free.
In the case of doctors serving in military hospitals, are they paid a salary or fees, or how are they remunerated?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They may serve on salary, or they may serve part time on fees.

I should like to take this opportunity to make a brief reference to the work which is being dqne at the paraplegic centre in Toronto called Lyndhurst. The men at that institution are such as prior to this war and even during the war until very recently would be condemned to be bed-ridden for the rest of their lives. I am not qualified to discuss the medical aspects, but I have been there and seen the work done. The patients are men who have suffered spinal injuries during the war and who, I am told, until this school was established and the treatment made available, might have lived for some three to five years, but within a very short time would have died, and in the meantime would have been completely bed-ridden and helpless. Under the direction of Lieutenant-Colonel John Counsell, who is himself a paraplegic, a start has been made with special reference to veterans. They took over the large home at Lyndhurst and have a centre there which, I believe, the Department of Veterans Affairs is supporting very generously at the moment. Some tribute should be paid to the work which is being done there, because these
Supply-Veterans Affairs

ex-officers and men whom I have seen are able to get themselves out into their wheel chairs, move themselves around, in some cases even get themselves into and out of cars and taxis, and generally lead a life which, of course, is not a normal life but enables them to look after themselves much more than formerly they could do. I believe there is some trouble in that this centre is anxious to extend its work to include all paraplegics, veterans and others. It is the only existing centre in Canada for that work, and I understand that they have made representations that nonveterans cases be allowed in that centre, to receive the same treatment, and that the work be extended. I wonder if the minister could say whether consideration is being given to that or not, and also, when he makes a statement on it, if he would cover the point in connection with the amount payable by these veterans for their wheel chairs. I regret that I overlooked the facts when the Customs Tariff Act was being discussed. These chairs are manufactured only in the United States; they are a special type, of light aluminum construction, and collapsible, so that the veteran can easily manoeuvre the chair, and when he gets into a car or taxi the chair is capable of being folded up and put in the back trunk. It is not manufactured in Canada; it has to be imported from the United States, and duty is payable on it. I intended to raise this matter when the Customs Tariff Act was before the house and ask that these chairs be exempted from duty. Perhaps the minister would bring it to the attention of the Department of Finance with a view of having these chairs exempted from duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for his remarks. I, too, have been through Lyndhurst Lodge. In regard to the wheel chairs, they are purchased and maintained by the department.
This institution for paraplegics is founded upon Mill Hill, in England; and the results have been simply amazing. Perhaps I should give one or two figures to the committee. It is only a small place, with a bed capacity of thirty-seven. At present there are twenty-eight paraplegic patients. The total number of patients who have been to the lodge is sixty, of whom thirty-nine are now out doing useful work or at school. A very limited number of civilian cases are being admitted on a repayment basis from the provincial government. One such case is at the lodge at the present time,
I think a visit to this place is one of the most encouraging experiences in the world.

Men who were completely paralyzed and wholly disabled-at least sixty per cent of them-are now back at work.

My information is at
variance with the minister's. I was told that they had to pay for their chairs themselves, and that is why payment of the customs duty is important. If there has been a change recently I am glad to hear of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Not veterans. That
may be true of civilian patients, but not a single veteran has to pay for or maintain his wheel chair. He never has.

The vote for this particular item, treatment and services, is one of the utmost importance to soldiers and their dependents. Wide additions have been made in the several bills which were passed relating to this matter. The efficiency of our doctors and nurses in the last war-a matter to which I referred the other day in connection with one of the minister's bills-has been greatly increased in comparison with the first war, although it was splendid then. But there are some features of this treatment affecting outdoor patients and others who come under the scope of the several bills which call for attention. One or two expenditures are not included in the new bill. I understand it is the policy of the minister to apply this particular item to additional services. Will soldier's families and the dependents as well be included? There is some provision for dependents in one of the bills. One cannot but think of all the universities have done in connection with this item, the rapid strides in science, medicine and surgery which have been made, and the large numbers of doctors and nurses whose services in our hospitals here and overseas form a most commendable feature of this legislation. Do not forget that but for the veterans who enlisted in this war we should have had all the horrors of war on our own soil, in Ontario and Quebec and the other provinces; and the best treatment the minister can give these veterans and their families is none too good for them.
I appreciate what has been done by the universities to assist in connection with our Sunnybrook hospital, upon the erection of which about $18 million will be spent. It is going to be an important institution, and special types of cases from all parts of Ontario and other parts of the country are being dealt with. I notice that the cost of the furniture and many other items for this hospital is being contributed voluntarily-a most commendable feature. I do not see that

Supply-Veterans Affairs
being done in other hospitals throughout the country. Large amounts of equipment, including chairs for amputation cases and many other features which will add to the comfort of the patients, are being collected1, and something is being done for the benefit of outdoor patients. I think a general principle should be applied with regard to the treatment of these cases and the provision of these services.
In addition, I find that there is much complaint from some of the soldiers' families and some of the inmates about the lack of treatment, and the equality of service provided under this item, which I hope will be applied to all who served, in addition to the imperials.
I was very much surprised at the action which was taken this morning as announced by one of our ministers. I appreciate that it does not come under this item, but let me say that it is going to cause wide disunity in this country, and I do not know of anything which will lead to more trouble than this order in council. It should be repealed and annulled.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
My hon. friend mentioned treatment for dependents. There are treatment allowances for dependients, but not treatment as such.
In regard to the Sunnybrook hospital, we intend to move patients in there immediately, with a gradual infiltration of patients as the construction and establishment of staff develop to completion.

I hesitate to say even a few words since I am not a veteran of either the first or the last great war. But at this time I should like to refer to something which has been in my mind on other occasions when veterans matters were before this house. In my humble opinion, of all committees dealing with veterans or other affairs which have ever worked in this house, no committee, from my experience of it, deserves as much credit as the veterans committee which we have had this session. They certainly did good work; they had in mind only one thing, as far as I could see from their reports, and that was to do everything possible in the interests of the veterans of both wars. After saying that, I have no criticism to make, but I would point, out to the minister that in our province the situation is rather different from that in other parts of the dominion. As the minister knows, he gave us a grant for two hospitals there. These, of course, even when the buildings are completed, will not be quite sufficient to accommodate the veterans who are seeking hospitalization, and when the veterans have to go to the other provinces the inconvenience
is great not only to themselves but also to their relatives at home. If from time to time we appeal to the Minister of Veterans Affairs in special cases, all I am asking for at the present time, without any criticism whatever, it that he will look into our isolated conditions there.

You will be welcome.

This is the first item dealing with pensions, and I wish to raise the question of making available to pensioners some extra payment in recognition of the increase in the cost of living. I have seen correspondence between the minister or officials of the department and those who raise the question, and the answer given by the department is that when the pensions were first instituted they were found to be not sufficient and a cost of living bonus was added thereto between the years 1919 and 1925. In 1925, although I am not quite certain of the year, this cost of living bonus was incorporated in the pension itself, and the answer is given that there is already an increase in the basic rates to take care of the increased cost of living. I do not 	iflfiTT
think that is strictly accurate, because it must be admitted that the cost of living has recently increased over the period before the war, and in the case of civil service salaries that increase has recently been recognized in the form of cost of living bonus which is now incorporated in the civil servant's salary. In the same way these pensioners feel that they should have a cost of living bonus. In their case it is more important than in the case of civil servants or anyone who is not a pensioner. The reason is that a pensioner, because of his disability, is less able to increase his earnings to take care of the increase in the cost of living. He is getting a pension because he is disabled, and because he is disabled he cannot go out and get extra work or look for a new job at higher wages. So that many of these men are finding themselves in actual hardship because of the increased cost of living. I know the Canadian Legion has brought this matter to the attention of the department, and I should like to know the attitude the minister takes.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My hon. friend is making himself thoroughly popular, of course, and I am going to make myself thoroughly unpopular in my reply. In 1919 a bonus of twenty per cent was authorized for the basic rate of pension then in force, $600 per annum, bringing the rate of pension for total disability to $720 per annum. The cost of living index was then 126-5. In 1920 the bonus was increased to fifty per cent, making the rate of pension for total disability $900 per annum. The cost of living index was then 145-4. This rate remained in effect until 1925, when the bonus was incorporated into the rate of pension, which has remained the same ever since, namely $900. The cost of living index in 1925 had been reduced to 119-8. According to the latest available information, the cost of living index as at July 1, 1946, was 125-1 as against 145-4 in 1920.
In 1920 did they have the same basic year they had in 1946?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: These varying rates in the cost of living index are supplied by the bureau of statistics from year to year. I have given several years; I mentioned 1919, 1920, 1925 and then 1946.
But may I ask what is the basic year for the 1920 figure?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The bonus was increased to fifty per cent, making the rate of pension $900 per annum. The cost of living index was then 145-4.

But when we are discussing the basic rate of $900 per annum, it should be made clear that this amount, which is $75

Supply-Veterans Affairs
a month, is the maximum pension; that is to say, the pension for total disability. A man who is 100 per cent disabled gets $75 a month.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: A single man.
Yes. I do not think this thing should be looked at from the point of view of-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Of course, if he is totally disabled he may have some allowance for helplessness as well.

Yes, if he requires a fulltime nurse. The point is that the pension for 100 per cent disability is $75 a month. I do not think this thing should be looked at from the point of view of whether we are going to make ourselves good fellows or bad fellows, or popular or unpopular. If the minister thinks I am doing this to make myself popular I can only say the government must have added the cost of living bonus to the salaries of civil servants in order to make itself popular.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am informed by my colleague that the cost of living basic index is based upon 1913.

That is not relevant to what I am saying at the moment. I think this matter should be looked at from the point of view of whether or not a man can support himself on the scale of pension he now receives. I do not think it can be said that $75 a month is over-generous for a man who is 100 per cent disabled. The point I was making was that if the cost of living goes up, these disabled men suffer more than a person who is not disabled, because by reason of their disability they are less able to make casual earnings to take care of the increased cost of living. The minister in his answer has referred to the points which I said had already been raised! in reply to the representations from the legion, and I take it that is the final decision, that there will be no increase to offset the higher cost of living?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is nothing final in the mysterious processes of government.

I want to ask whether any money is provided under this item for imperials. Some of these men have been living here for thirty years. When the first great war broke out they went Overseas and1 enlisted of their own volition, though they were Canadians then and have been ever since. I should like to see some provision made for hospital treatment for themselves and their families, and as to rate of exchange in pay. Some of them are in very bad condition; it is almost pitiable to see them. Here we are spending all these millions; and the people who went to
fight in the first war, even though they were imperials and even though many of them have been living in Canada for forty years, get nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Again being unpopular, I must abide by the principle I have always maintained, that unless these imperials were domiciled in Canada before they served with the imperial or other forces, they should not have precedence over Canadians who were born in this country and who do not get these benefits. We have quite a number of Canadians who went to England but through no fault of their own were not able to get to France; that was during the first war. Unless they are pensioners they do not qualify for the war veterans' allowance; and I think this committee must deal with them and give them recognition before any others who come from any other country, no matter how gallantly they have served the empire, are given these benefits which our own Canadians do not get. I have taken that stand consistently, and as long as I am head of this department I intend to abide by it. I realize it is not popular, but I think it is right.
If they had deserted they would have got a gold watch and an illuminated address from this parliament.

In the riding of Davenport we have quite a number who, I suppose, would come under the heading of imperial soldiers; they were soldiers before they came here prior to 1914, and lived in that riding for four or five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Then they were domiciled here and they are protected.
Rut when the war broke out they went to England and enlisted.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They are protected.
As long as they were living here before the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They are treated the same as Canadian if they were domiciled here in 1914, before going to war. They are protected.
Even if they served in the imperial forces?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, absolutely; or in the allied forces of His Majesty.

As the minister no doubt knows, a new type of cheque is being issued to pensioners, made of a sort of semi-cardboard, which is quite stiff and which bears a notice saying, "Do not fold." This means it is not possible for a man to put the cheque in
Supply-Veterans Affairs

his pocketbook. I have had a number of complaints in this connection, and I should like to ask the minister whether these complaints are general, to his knowledge.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am glad to hear that complaint from my hon. friend. I understand the cheque in question is not issued by the Canadian pension commission but by the treasury as such.

If not, will the minister explain the item, and also indicate the number who received assistance last year, and to date this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This has nothing to do with out-of-work benefits. This is an old vote which, if my memory is correct, was established in 1932 to meet unemployment conditions prevailing at that time in connection with those in the various branches of the department across Canada who needed assistance. It was our hope that it would be abolished, but unfortunately we have not yet been able to have it abolished, with the result that, to a certain extent, it still exists.
Does it now include any amount for unemployed soldiers? I notice that the mayor and board of control of Toronto have been complaining about the large number of soldiers there out of work.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

world war I, $750,000.
Why is there an increase in this item? It would seem to stand to reason that there would be fewer veterans qualifying now than there were a year ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am informed that there is a gradual increase, and that this is to be expected on account of the age of a number of the pensioners from world war I receiving treatment in our hospitals.
They would all be cases of pensioners?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

I should like at this point to refer to Mr. Walter Callow in Camp Hill hospital, Nova Scotia. I should imagine the minister has received some communication from him. This man has been absolutely crippled, and is blind; they call him the stone man. He cannot move. But, as I remember, through his efforts some thousands of cigarettes were obtained for soldiers overseas.
Millions.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Hundreds of thousands, probably millions.

Mr. Callow has designed a carrier for wheel chairs for the purpose of taking crippled soldiers to sports events. Has the department in any way encouraged him in this matter? The other day I noticed in a United States paper an article which said that they were designing carriers to take their helpless patients to such events. I was wondering whether our department had considered Mr. Callow's suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I believe I know Mr. Callow as well as most people do, and I know he has been doing marvellous work for the last twenty or twenty-five years. However, those who are in charge of the paraplegic curative treatment do not consider the chair he has designed to be the most effective.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
It is a carrier, not a chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What is required is a chair which can be placed in an automobile. Although they are most grateful to him for the work he has done, they do not at the present time recommend the design he has submitted.
I do not know that Mr. Callow has asked the government to assist. He has been seeking private donations, I believe; whether he has made application to the government for assistance, I cannot say.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: None.

I am glad the hon. member for Royal has mentioned Mr. Callow. On more than one occasion I have gone on record as advocating every possible assistance to him. I believe, too, that the hon. member for Peel has added his word to those of other hon. members. I sincerely trust that the minister will give every possible consideration to this veteran, not only because of his physical condition, but because of the splendid effort he put forth driving the recent war to help make easier the lives of those who, like him, have been disabled. In ' addition, he performed splendid work by providing cigarettes by the millions for those overseas.
I would suggest that we could provide him with more suitable quarters at Camp Hill. I know the minister has had this matter under his personal supervision, and has been sympathetic toward it. May I point out that there is an office at present not occupied which this veteran could use to further the cause which he has supported.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I shall be glad to take that into my personal consideration at once. As regards the design which has been submitted, the official finding of the department- rightly or w'rongly-is that we require folding, collapsible chairs, which will go into the ordinary motor car. His design is somewhat different, but the matter is worthy of further consideration.

Perhaps I should have asked on an earlier item the question I am about to ask. However, I 'would point out that I have received letters, mostly from veterans of world war I, who are receiving partial pensions, requesting that they be given a cost of living allowance. I could bring a number of cases to the minister's attention. I might refer to one case of a man, the father of four or five children, who is receiving a thirty per cent disability pension and! who is unable to work for more than twenty-five per cent of the time.
Pensioners in that position are having a difficult time to get along these days, and in view of the fact that almost every other department is receiving a cost of living bonus,
I was w'ondering if the minister had given consideration to extending that cost of living bonus to pensioners in world wars I and II.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is difficult to give a decisive answer on a question such as has been asked by the hon. member. If the pension is inadequate, the pensioner can apply for a war veterans allowance, and thereby augment the assessment to meet living conditions.

I should like to add to what has been said by the hon. member for Royal and the senior hon. member for Halifax with respect to Mr. Walter Callow. Mr. Callow comes from my constituency of Cumberland and has been hospitalized since the last war. I believe that he has suffered as greatly as anyone who came out of that war. Those who have had contact with Mr. Callow's work know he has done wonderful things since the last war, and especially during the period of this war. Not only has he assisted in securing funds for cigarettes, but he has suggested a major government policy with respect to hospitalization. He proposes that more attention should be given to improving the equipment in local hospitals as opposed to concentrating on the larger hospitals in cities such as Halifax, Montreal, Toronto and other places. He feels that the returned men would get better attention and be much happier if they were accommodated in the smaller hospitals rather than all being concentrated in the larger institutions. I am very much in sympathy with the policy proposed by Mr. Callow, and I hope that the minister will give it more attention from now on and carry it out, if at all possible. It would be a good thing, not only for the returned men but for the smaller hospitals which are struggling to carry on with their very necessary operations.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I shall be very happy to look into the matter.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I realize that this matter has been discussed this year both in the committee on veterans affairs and also when the bill amending the War Veterans Allowances Act was before the house, and- I suppose we have obtained from the government about all that we can hope for this year. However, I feel that this item should not be allowed to pass without some of us stating again to the minister and to the government that we hope next year the amounts paid under these allowances will be raised to at least $40 per month. I hope the minister will continue to give his sympathetic consideration-and I hope it will

produce results-the other requests made by and on behalf of these widows. Without excluding the others, I refer particularly to hospitalization because that is one thing they are vitally concerned about. I urge that something be done about this matter at an early day.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not usually agree with my hon. friend, but I would point out that this vote is for $1,800,000, and it was all done in the last year largely, if I may say so, through the advocacy of the hon. member for Davenport, of the hon. member who has just spoken and, of course, because of the sympathy and generosity of this house.
What is the annual payment per month?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
$31.40 per month; try to live on that.
May I ask again if consideration is being given to the question of hospitalization?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: At the present time and for some time to come we shall require all our hospital space for the men who have been fighting. Until the peak of this need for treatment goes down, we cannot give any consideration to providing treatment for anybody else.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am afraid the minister does not understand what these women are asking for. Many of these women are of an age when they have to be taken into hospitals, not those administered by the department but into civilian hospitals. The problem is one of allowances to cover expenses, not one of providing space in a departmental hospital.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I may be making myself thoroughly unpopular this evening, but I say I am against that until the soldiers themselves are completely looked after.

I do not know whether the minister at any time during the discussion has given the committee a statement of the government's policy with respect to widows of non-pensionable war veterans and, if he

Supply-Veterans Affairs
has not, I should like to have this. Many widows of veterans of the last war are in needy circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In the first place, certain widows are entitled to pensions as a matter of right. A year ago this house in its wisdom gave attention to what we call nonpensionable widows, and we are providing SI,800,000 in the present estimates for them. At the risk of being criticized, we say that we have been pretty generous.
I do not think the minister should be criticized.

I do not think we can say we have been pretty generous. I have in mind a widow of a veteran who asked to go overseas during the last war but who was kept here. This man finally died as the result of injuries received. This widow has done everything in her power to raise her family and take care of herself. She is highly qualified for various kinds of work, but she is having the greatest difficulty in finding any work to do. I do not know that this committee can feel that it has been generous to the veterans of the last war so long as we leave widows of that kind to suffer around the country. I do not look upon ourselves as being generous at all. Of course there are those who say the government has no responsibility to them. But I think the country has, and that is why I am appealing to the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I was impressed, when this war opened, with the statement that was made in several places. I believe it was made first by a prominent official in New Zealand and then it was repeated by several officials in Canada, that no one should be any worse off because he went to war and no one should be any better off because he did not go to war. I think that is a pretty sound principle. A woman in this position is certainly worse off because her husband went to war, and I shall not feel happy about the matter until some policy is laid down whereby we can give more assistance to widows of this type than we are giving.

I do not think we should let this item pass without saying a word on behalf of the minister. From the very beginning I supported this movement to give non-pensioned widows a pension which they richly deserve, and from the very beginning the minister has been sympathetic at all times to pensioning non-pensioned widows. If he had been opposed to it, we never would have got very far in our efforts for these widows, and so far as I am concerned I feel disposed to thank the minister on behalf of those I am associated with for having gone as far as he
has. But, of course, like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I hope he will go farther by and by.

461. Pensions, North West rebellion, 1885 and general, $15,000.
How many of these pensioners are there?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Including the militia service pension and the additional allowance which this house has made in the last couple of years, there are 12,249.
There are 12,249 pensioners of the North West rebellion?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is militia pensions, plus our pensions.

I understood, when I was before the committee, that something would be done for the veterans who served in the North West rebellion in 1885. I understood that there was going to be a real clean-up this year of our debt to all these veterans who have served their country. They were the pioneers and predecessors of the present militia. They came from Halifax and the midland counties and from all over Ontario and the Ottawa district and1 the 90th of Winnipeg, and they have never got a cent except under the small amendment that was made last year. Last year's vote of $16,000 has now been cut down to $15,000 for "Pensions, North West rebellion, 1885 and general." I should like to know what is the distinction between the North West field force and "general". These veterans have been granted practically nothing, and it would be almost better to strike out the item than to continue the means test. I admit that an order in council was passed last session providing a very small sum of money for these veterans. They marched in the depths of winter, when it was thirty and forty degrees below zero, across the country around lake Superior before the Canadian Pacific railway was completed. They came from Halifax, the maritimes, Ontario, Winnipeg, to the defence of the prairie provinces and they were responsible for this country not being dislocated. They have been forgotten from 1885 down to to-day, except for a small grant of land hardly any of them ever see. A very small vote was put in the estimates last year, and I give the minister great credit for that, but the way it was applied it did not mean very much, if anything. It would have been far better to strike it out altogether than to apply the means test to these people. The test is well named. They should have received
Supply-Veterans Affairs

the same allowance as the South African veterans got as a right, not as charity. I have been told the reason why they were not treated the same. I do not like to say what the reason is, but I have been told some of the reasons.
I pleaded with the select committee for these veterans, and I want to give credit to that committee, which included members from all sides of the house, for the various bills as to veterans which they recommended to the house. That committee forgot about party politics in the nine bills and they seem to have forgotten all about the North West rebellion. There is no reference to it in the eight or nine veterans bills that passed this house. Why are these men discriminated against?
I met the widow of one of these veterans the other day. She is getting about $29 a month in old age pension. Under this vote she would have been entitled to $39. She wrote me about the matter and I told her to stick to the old age pension since they were to deduct from the $39 the $29 old age receipts. The result, was that she got nothing for 1885. Her husband was one of the finest members of the press in Canada.
It is no credit to our country so to forgot these veterans and to leave these people to the municipalities. That is where they are left, and they get put out of their homes. I know one veteran who lost his books, his desk, his household goods and everything. His house was sold and he never got a nickel. These men had a reunion in June, 1945, on the anniversary of their enlistment. It is a mean way for parliament to treat these men when we are voting $51,000,000 on these various other items for veterans and dependents. I am surprised that members from the other provinces of Canada do not rise and speak on behalf of these veterans. Many of them came from Halifax in the maritime provinces, and they were known as Haligonians. Many of these men are living to-day and they are not in good circumstances. Others came from the other provinces. We owe a debt of gratitude which is long overdue to these people who did so much for the prairie provinces in 1885 before the Canadian Pacifc railway was completed. They should have more supporters than they have in this house when, this item is called. The hon. member for Peel has been a very warm friend of these men. He has veterans of the North West rebellion in his riding, as have the Toronto members. But outside of him, the hon. member for Davenport and the hon. member for York South, we hear little from other members in
favour of these veterans. The means test is well named. It is mean to use the veterans of this country in this way. They are the men who built up the militia in Canada from 1885 on-the old Grenadiers, the Queen's Own, the Body Guard, commanded by Colonel Denison, the Midland Battalion. Tributes and assistance for these men are long overdue. They were the very back-bone of our present militia, and their sons and grandsons served in the South African war and the two great wars.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I must take emphatic exception to my hon. friend's remarks in regard to these old veterans. I have found out that 114 veterans, as a result of what this house did during the last two years, are drawing $54,000, and forty widows are drawing $13,000. In regard to the regulations for the veterans allowance, they are exactly the same for them as they are for those who fought in the first great war. So that I do not think we have been unkind. The total annual obligation arising from what we did here last year is $66,877.

I am not going to talk about the Riel rebellion. There are two matters to which I was going to refer under pensions. Unfortunately I was in the industrial relations committee and did not get the chance, so that I should like to say a word on them here.
The first is the matter which I discussed with the pension committee back in 1940. It has reference to a woman divorcing her husband: in the United1 States; he resides -in Canadia. In this case, after the man was divorced in the United States he re-married in Canada, supposing that he had been legally divorced,. He obtained a licence and' was married in a church. The woman lived with him for twenty-six years. He died last year. Despite the fact that she went through all the legal machinery provided in Canada, including a church wedding, in marrying this man, the Pension Act is such that it is held that she was not legally married to this man. I raised the matter on several occasions. I discussed it with the former Minister of Justice, the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, back in 1940 and 1941. He said it might necessitate a change in the divorce laws of Canada and, the war then being on, they did not want to disturb the existing machinery. At this session in the veterans affairs committee the matter was discussed briefly, and I thought that, where there were extenuating circumstances such as I have just described, the commission would be given sufficient latitude to adjudicate a matter of that kind. So I wrote the chainman of the commission and

Supply-Veterans Affairs
he searched the records, and concluded that no latitude was given the commission. That case still stands in abeyance. I was wondering whether the minister could not devise some ways and means of qualifying that widow for a pension. The pensioner with whom she lived had a seventy-five per cent disability. Now that he is dead', she is left at the mercy of the world.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Is the hon. member referring to the Adams or the Mackenzie case?

The Adams case. The Mackenzie case is only brief; it has to do with an old soldier who, having remarried in 1944, finds that he can not include his wife in the pension. He is practically living on her. Is there anything we can do about that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
First of all, in regard' to the Mackenzie case, as the committee will remember, this question of a deadline was thoroughly discussed in the pension committee and it was decided, and affirmed by this house, that in the case of a marriage after the first of May, 1944, no pension could be given with respect to that wife or widow; however, if the marriage took place before that, and children were born after that deadline, a pension should be paid in respect of them. At the present time there is no way in which Mr. Mackenzie can get a pension in respect of his wife, or his widow if he should unfortunately pass away.
Mr. G I'LL 18: I merely used that case as an illustration. It is a general problem.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Of course, as the law stands at present, the commission is bound by that. The Adams case is the case where this gentleman was domiciled in Canada, and was married; his wife abandoned him and went to the United States and divorced him in the state of Vermont, I understand, on grounds which would not be recognized as valid for a divorce in Canada. So the situation is this, that in the first place the divorce was not valid in Canada because the divorce at that time had to be based on the domicile of the husband, and if the woman had tried to get the divorce in Canada she could not have got it because there were not grounds. Then this gentleman married somebody else after his wife had divorced him. At any time he could have got a divorce in Canada on the basis of what his wife had done, but he did not choose to do it, so that his marriage was not valid in Canada.

Well, why was he not
arrested for bigamy? He lived for twenty-six years with that woman.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That, of course, is another question; it is a matter of the criminal code. Nevertheless, the marriage was not valid. The committee may be interested to know why we adhere to that view. We do so because, if we permitted people to go away and get divorces which are not valid in Canada, and come back to Canada, we might have disputes in respect of several wives. The question is, which wife would you recognize, unless you go by the law of Canada?
Are you not getting into a bit of trouble here?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No, I am not. I am being very careful, and trying to point out why the law is not changed. Generally it is the husband who leaves and goes to the United States and gets a divorce which is not valid in Canada; then he comes back to Canada and marries here. Of course, under Canadian law his first wife is his lawful wife; but if you decided, regardless of the law of Canada, that you would pay a pension with respect to the second wife, you would have the first wife and perhaps her children left in a difficult position. So we felt that the only safe way to go is by the law of Canada as regards whom our law recognizes as his wife and children. No doubt it leads to difficult cases, which we recognized in the committee, and it is unfortunate that there is not some way of taking care of these cases where there is good faith, where the woman marries thinking she is going through a valid marriage, for, of course, it makes it very difficult. I hope that some way will be found to take care of these real good faith cases without having to enter into the more difficult field of complicated matrimonial relations.

I agree with the parliamentary assistant as to his general premise; but in the Adams case I do not think it is applicable, because, to begin with, Adams' wife deserted him while he was overseas, and when he came back she was in the United States and had secured a divorce. He was a rank and file soldier, and not knowing all the legal machinery of the country he assumed he was single. He secured a licence from the government agency.
Of what province?

Nova Scotia. He went to a church and he was married as legally as he could be. As to his securing a Canadian divorce on the ground that his first wife had deserted him and committed misconduct through her other marriage, the financial obligation enters the picture. He would require money; he would have to serve papers on her in the United States. That was probed
Supply-Veterans Affairs

on several occasions, but financially he could not undertake that obligation, so that the matter slid along. I am not concerned about him; he has gone to the great beyond, but he leaves behind him a woman with whom he lived for twenty-six years.
Any children?
No.
Well, then, she is all right.

She is at an age to-day when she is something like ourselves, ornamental but not very useful. I am now making this suggestion to the minister, and perhaps this is the only case of the kind in Canada. I am reasonably sure that if the minister, the parliamentary assistant and the pension chairman got their heads together they could devise ways and means of granting a pension to this widow. I agree with the hon. member for Rosthern that you have to protect the people of the country against wholesale divorces and so on, but there is absolutely no doubt that there are extenuating circumstances in this case. Even if the minister would pass an order in council quietly-
Can that be done?

Even if he did that, and said that in cases such as the Adams case, taking that as a base-and I am giving the chairman of the commission administrative latitude if certain circumstances prevail-a pension will be granted, it would fix the thing up. I shall be keeping in touch with this widow because I certainly hope that the minister will do as I suggest.
Under what item does the vote come for the South African veterans?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Under war veterans allowances.

To come back to item 461, pensions in connection with the North West rebellion, I was interested in the minister's remarks with regard to the beneficent way in which the government had treated these chaps.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not use that word.

Well, the minister implied that he had been very generous, that the department had spent a great deal of money. One of these chaps happens to live in my own town. I know him quite well, and for some time I followed the discussion with regard to the efforts that have been made by those concerned to get a pension for their service in the North West rebellion. That is

exactly sixty-one years ago, and most of these chaps are over the age limit. They are now, to use the expression of my hon. friend the member for Cape Breton South, merely ornamental.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I was not here then.
But the minister was here later on, administering the department when he could give a pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And I got it for them.

When did it go
through?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Two years ago.

I remember the last day of the session when the minister rose in his place and announced with great gusto the fact that at last a regulation had been passed granting these noble veterans of 1885 a splendid pension to take care of them for the rest of their days.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I never used the words "splendid pension". That is only C.C.F. exaggeration.

On arriving back home, I met this chap and I said to him, "You will be pleased to know that the Liberal government has seen fit to grant you people a pension for your services in 1885". He replied, "You know, they have been very good to me because I got that long envelope containing an intimation that they were going to give me a pension for my services in 1885; but, strange to say, I also received notification at the same time that my old age pension was being cut off because I was getting money from another source".

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Who cut it off-the provincial government, the C.C.F.?

The minister's own regulations did. If it is intended that these men shall get some special benefit, if the minister wishes to try to help them, he can pass regulations, or have them passed, to provide that the miserable pittance they receive shall not be assessable as income.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I interrupt
without being unkind? The treatment they have received is exactly the same as that received by the 24,000 battle veterans of the first great war.
But they were not getting old age pensions.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
They are all treated in the same way.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
Yes, but the others did not fall within the category of old age pensioners. It meant absolutely nothing to these men.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is no difference in treatment.

It is of no use at all to these men. The veteran of the first great war is not receiving an old age pension. This man at one time was receiving an old! age pension and then is given a pension in recognition of services rendered in 18S5, but if he accepts the one he has to do without the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is $30 a month now, whereas before it was $20.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It is wrong to say that there is no advantage under the war veterans allowances. If he is a married man and even if his wife is not over 70 years of age, under this legislation he can get $730. He is permitted to have an income above that of $250, without affecting the allowance-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Yes, and he he can get an income of $250 above that without affecting the allowance. He is permitted casual earnings of $125, an income from investments of $25 a year, and he is permitted to own a home worth $4,000, without affecting the war veterans allowance. That is much better than old age pension, as the hon. member knows, and when he says it is not an advantage he is saying something that is not correct.
It made no difference to this man.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: In the case of a single man, he can get $365 a year. He is permitted to have earnings of $125 above that, casual earnings of $125; he is permitted to have $25 a year from investments and a home worth $4,000.
If he can earn it at the age of eighty-one.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I am saying that it is better than an old age pension and many people prefer to have the allowance rather than the old age pension. I do not think, therefore, that it can be said that the people who worked to get this advantage-and they knew what the terms were under which it would be paid-did not get something of an advantage, to the northwest field force veteran. I do not think it is fair to say that nothing was obtained1 for them.
It certainly is wrong for the minister to claim that it was a piece of generosity. In this case it meant nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Give us the concrete details of that case.
I shall be glad to give it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Give it to the committee now.
The name is Caldwell.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not want the name. Give the committee the particulars of the allowances which that man had before and the allowance he received as a result of what the house did two years ago. I want the amount right now, because it is not true.
I gave you the name.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not want the name but I do want the particulars. If my hon. friend makes a statement on the floor of the house, that we did not increase that man's allowances, I want to know what he was receiving previously under the old age pension, which was cancelled, and what he received through the act of this parliament.
I shall be glad to give it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I want it now.
You have the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No; I want it now.
I think I understand the hon. member for Yorkton quite well. It works the same in all these cases.
No.
Sit down.
Listen-
Sit down.
A new leader.
Not at all.
I thought you were working for the widows.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Cape Breton South has the floor.
This sounds like the industrial relations committee where, the moment you say something that may settle the strike, they all begin to ishout about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Give us the facts.

The minister knows that what was given the North West rebellion people was a pension of $10 a month. These fellows are old; you have to be old to get the old age pension. He receives in any province in Canada $20 a month old age pension after he passes seventy years of age. This is the condi-
Supply-Veterans Affairs

tion of these old heroes who stormed lake Superior, and I am giving the government credit for what it has done, because the matter was neglected for sixty years under similar governments. The present government decided to do something about the matter, and granted a pension of $30 a month to the old veterans of the North West rebellion. To the committee which came to that decision I give full credit; but immediately that happened the provincial government cut off the $20 a month old age pension, so that these old gentlemen benefited to the extent of $10 a month. That is the case in every province of Canada. It not only applies to pensioners of that class; it applies also to those under war veterans allowances, and it applied to the soldier in the service who made an assignment to his old father and mother. Immediately the assignment was made, the $20 was cut off.
Mr. GRANT; No.

Oh, yes. I could give you case after case of that, where the minute the pension was granted by the federal government for a son who was killed overseas, the old age pension was discontinued. That is something we shall have to iron out in this house some time.
But not in the case of an assignment. It may be so in the case of a pension.

It was done in connection with pay and allowances, too, all over the shop. I had case after case; some I straightened out and some I could not. That is the long and short of the story. Through this government we granted them $30 a month; the provincial governments cut off $20, and they benefited to the extent of $10. I hope the veterans affairs committee will reconvene next session so that we may straighten out the provincial government in that regard.

Soldier Settlement and Veterans' Land Act-
464. Administration of soldier settlement, British family settlement, general land settlement and Veterans' Land Act, including engineering and other investigational planning and subdivision expenses that do not add tangible value to real property, $5,443,400.

I should like to refer briefly to a condition which exists in the Hamilton area and, I believe, is general throughout Ontario, in connection with the transfer of properties. I understand that all the legal work in connection with the transfer of property is being done by one very learned gentleman, Mr. W. C. Thomson, K.C., of Toronto, and that a serious bottleneck exists at the moment, with the result that veterans have to wait for months before they get the transfer of these properties. Recently an article appeared in the Hamilton Spectator relating to this matter, and I should like to read part of it:
The bottleneck has become so choked that representations have been made to officials at Ottawa protesting "extended delays" . . .
Further on it says:
Registry office here is admitted to be working long hours at top speed to get these abstracts out so that the transfers may be completed. However, the criticism is that local solicitors could make the searches, establish clear title to a property, and save the veteran weeks or even months of time in settling on his land.
And finally the article states:
Local lawyers were unanimous that the fault was not in Hamilton but at Toronto or officialdom at Ottawa.
Wilfred R. Hobson. K.C., said the delays were "becoming worse." Arthur Treleaven said that he had written three letters to the Toronto office since June 7, and had not received an answer.
In conclusion, may I say that this criticism is not in any sense political, because the first named learned gentleman is a Conservative, while the last named is a member of an honoured Liberal family in the city of Hamilton.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
