My hon. friend is not the first to bring this matter to my attention.

Supply-Veterans Affairs

There are no reflections whatsoever upon the ability or integrity of Mr. Thompson, the criticisms are that there is too much centralization and occasionally there may be some delay in the clearing of titles at local centres. The suggestion has been made that local legal gentlemen should clear these titles, and the matter is now receiving active consideration.

On August 1 last I promised the leader of the opposition that I would give him exact information with regard to the cost of the small holdings, and I think I should carry out that undertaking though the hon. gentleman is not in the house at the moment. The questions were: (a) how many of these houses will cost the state less than $6,000; (b) how many will cost the state more than $6,000; (c) what is the estimated average excess cost of the whole project over S6.000 each?
Contracts were let for the construction of a total of 2,706 houses on subdivision projects across the dominion, 2,440 on a cost plus fixed fee per unit basis and 266 on a firm bid per unit basis. To date a total of 1,175 houses have come under final review by the committee composed of the deputy minister of veterans affairs and the director under the Veterans' Land Act. Of the houses, 609 cost the state less than $6,000; the average cost of construction was $5,574. The other 566 houses cost the state more than $6,000; the average cost of construction was $6,394. The average net cost of the total unit inclusive of house, land and all services is $7,058.
With the permission of the committee, I should like to place on record a summarized statement of the net cost to the state of these 1,175 small holding units. They represent forty separate projects in six provinces. It is not considered practicable to give the estimated net cost of the remainder of the houses under construction with the desired degree of accuracy. The remainder of 1,531 houses are in various stages of construction, with many near completion. It is estimated that all houses will have been completed by October 31 of this year. On completion of the remainder of these projects it will be possible to place on record a table similar to that which I am now filing. The statement I wish to have permission to place on record gives an exact statement of the various projects, the number that cost under $6,000 and the cost of same, the number that cost over $6,000 and the cost of same, so that all this information may be available to members of the committee.

Something has been said about the rental, with the idea that these houses were costing the veterans far more than perhaps they should. I might give the committee some information on that, for such use as they may wish to make of it. Where the adjusted cost to the director is $4,500, after the veteran has paid his ten per cent and gets his conditional write-off, the monthly rate he has to pay for twenty-five years in order to retire that contract is $14.92. If the adjusted cost to the director is $5,000, after the veteran gets his conditional write-off and pays his ten per cent his monthly cost is $16.58. If the suggested cost to the director is $5,500, that house will cost $18.24 to the veteran. If the cost is $6,000, the cost to the veteran, after he has made his down payment, is $19.90. If it is $6,500, in the event he pays $600 down, and when he gets his additional write-off, the amount he must pay for a $6,500 house is $22.39. If it is a $7,000 house he pays $600 down, and then pays a monthly amount of $24.88. If it a $7,500 house he pays $600 down, again, and his monthly payment is $27.57.
Those are figures which I believe will meet any apprehension on the part of hon. members that veterans are being asked to make payments which are out of line with rental payments in connection with other projects throughout Canada.

Mr. C tUICKSHANK: I want to know whether tiis annuity of $5,000 can be paid to one individual, when we can only pay our veterans $30 a month as a war veterans allowance. That will hold Prince Edward Island for a little while!
I was trying to help you out.

I do not need any help in this case. I am one who believes that credit has not been given as it should have been to the minister who comes from my province, and happens to be Minister of Veterans Affairs, for what he has done for the veterans of Canada. I am prepared to go back before my legion and any other legion and give that credit. But I am asking the minister at the same time to explain that $5,000 annuity to one Colonel Thompson. That is my first question.
My second question-and I will have to put these glasses on; I just paid $17 for them- affects soldier settlers. As I understand it, under the new act which was brought down, a man living in an outlying district is not eligible under the Veterans' Land Act for a house or home. I have an instance in Burnaby, in my own province, although I do not live in that area. I am giving the minister's officials plenty of time to look this up, Mr. Chairman, because I think they cannot answer it. But, as I understand the situation, a veteran in an area such as Burnaby-and I am instancing Burnaby or North Vancouver-is not eligible for a home, and I want to know why he is not.
The second question I wish to ask-
The third.

The third question -I am being helped a lot, and again I am taking plenty of time-is as to why homes now erected in Fraser Valley are not available for sale to veterans, and why veterans are not allowed to buy Japanese farms, homes or individual holdings in Fraser Valley, despite the fact that in the veterans affairs committee I was assured that these homes were available and would be made available for immediate sale to veterans.
I am definitely saying through you, Mr. Chairman, to the minister, that these Japanese farms in Fraser Valley are not being made available. These former Japanese homes in Fraser Valley are not being made available for sale. The veterans in my constituency do not know where they stand to-day in so far as purchasing homes is concerned, either those built under this veterans scheme or old homes and old farms taken over from the Japanese. I also wish to point out through you, Mr. Chairman, that no price has yet been set on
veterans homes in Fraser Valley, despite the fact that veterans were assured that these homes would not cost more than $4,800.
Again I would praise the minister and his assistant for the work they have done. But this government has made a mistake or has permitted a mistake to be made in connection with the cost of these homes. We must see that the veterans get them at a cost of $4,800, at which they expected to get them. That price was advertised in every paper in British Columbia. The statement was made on every platform in British Columbia in the last election-including the statement by the member for Fraser Valley-that these homes would be available at $4,800. The last figure I could get was anywhere from $5,800 to $6,400. When I ask for the actual cost I am told I can get an order for return-which will probably be returnable about six months or a year from now. That is not good enough, because neither the minister nor I might be here six months or a year from now, if they happen to have a by-election. I hope I shall be here.
I want to know and the veterans in my riding want to know when these homes will be available and what the actual cost will be. I was told that one reason the cost in British Columbia was higher was that we believe in paying reasonably decent wages in our province. I also asked at that time why lumber should cost more at Haney, where lumber is produced than it costs at Edmonton. I asked why cement should cost more in Fraser Valley, when it is produced in British Columbia, than it costs in Edmonton, Ottawa or elsewhere.
The minister has a lot of questions to answer; if he cannot answer them all immediately I hope he will keep a record of them. Perhaps he would answer by starting with Colonel Thompson and then work down the list. But I would ask particularly, if the minister has not sufficient staff to appraise these various homes and farm and houses, why he does not employ a greater staff in order that veterans from this war in Fraser Valley may acquire these homes and farms, settle on them, and become citizens of that part of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
My hon. friend, as usual, has asked a most intriguing series of questions. In the first place, in regard to properties in Fraser Valley, we had a report yesterday that we expect within the next ten days to have a sale price established for all the homes which have been constructed in Fraser Valley.
Next, with reference to Japanese homes, ninety former Japanese properties have been already sold to veterans and the remainder will be made available as quickly as possible.
Supply-Veterans Affairs

Next, with regard to Coloned John Thompson, he was chairman of the Canadian pension commission; when he retired, he was not entitled to superannuation allowance, and an amount was placed in the estimates, I believe of $5,000.
Then the hon. member asked about the Soldier Settlement Act. It is expected that that situation will be met in accordance with the wishes of my hon. friend.

I thank the minister for his answers. After six months of endeavour, I am hoping to go home next week and be able to tell the settlers in my riding that at last I have got a partial answer from the department. There are some 500 Japanese farms-
Former Japanese farms.

And they will
always be former Japanese farms. The minister now says that ninety have been sold. I want to know, when veterans of Fraser Valley and other parts of Canada are desiring to acquire these former Japanese homes, why only ninety have been made available for sale. I want definite assurance from the minister that the remainder of approximately 500 farms will be made available immediately.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The greatest demand for these farms has been from veterans with no overseas service, and it is the considered policy of the department to give preference to those who have been overseas.

I am not quarrelling with the minister's statement because I feel that overseas veterans should have the preference, but there are more than- 500 farms in my district, and I should like to know how long the limitations will remain and when these farms will be made available for veteran volunteers, not zombies but men with service in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is a submission now before the minister in regard to that matter.

I should like to say a few words with reference to the policy of administering the Veterans' Land Act. I brought this question up some time ago and it was partly discussed in the veterans committee. I am not bringing up this matter before the committee for the purpose of criticizing the government. The only motive I have in discussing this matter of veterans housing is to see that the veterans for whom I am speaking are given a square deal.
When this question first came up, the veterans in Calgary formed an association. Every

one of the veterans for whom I am speaking has had overseas sendee. When they first met there was a lengthy discussion as to the procedure that should be followed in order to get the necessary repairs and adjustments made to their property. It was suggested to them by me that as little publicity as possible be given to this matter and that every available effort be madie to go through the ordinary and proper channels to get the adjustments that were needed. The veterans were agreeable in that respect and they acted accordingly.
They interviewed everyone connected with the Veterans' Land Act in Calgary, and I think in Edmonton, but, I understand, with no results. Then, when the house opened I brought up the	question here. The minister was
acquainted with this problem before I brought it to the attention of the house. These men have done everything to have these things adjusted in the channels that rvere available to them before the matter was brought up here.
I am at a loss to know why the minister has seemed to be so hostile toward these adjustments. I can assure him that in regard to these houses I have never said anything that was not true. I have never exaggerated; in fact I hasten to say that I have never given as bad a picture as I might have had I gone into the matter more in detail. The question was brought up before the veterans affairs committee. Whether that committee could have gone into the study of the matter at greater length, I do not know because I was not a member of the committee. I should like to take this opportunity of referring to the proceedings of that committee for Monday, June 3, 1946. Mr. Murchison was the witness before the committee at that time, and he has this to say, as reported on page 769:
I can say frankly to this committee that with few exceptions the reaction of the public and veterans to this programme has been good, but there are a few exceptions which illustrate a lack of understanding of the difficulties of home construction at the present time, in some places a decided lack of appreciation of what the administration is trying to do and a tendency here and there to unfairly criticize which, to say the least, does not encourage very much expansion of building. I suggest to this committee there are plenty of places in Canada where our efforts thus far are fully appreciated and where there is still ample demand to fully absorb all the materials available for new construction. We have fortunately only a few samples of criticism of the type I referred to. Some of it developed in Calgary.
That was not answering my charge. I contend that on no occasion has Mr. Murchison ever given one instance where the things that I said in this house were not true. In

Supply-Veterans Affairs
fact, in my opinion Mr. Murchison did not have the information or, if he did, he did not reveal it to the committee. As I pointed out in the beginning, I have nothing to gain by this. I am not even seeking votes. It is not even in my constituency. The only thing I am concerned about is to see that proper treatment is meted out to these veterans who have served their country so well. Surely that is not asking too much. When Mr. Murchison makes this remark, "Where there is still ample demand to fully absorb all the materials available for new construction," he is threatening every veteran not to dare to criticize this policy, no matter what type of house he gets. I take the strongest possible objection to such a threat made against our returned men by any departmental official. Surely that is not the intention of the department. I am quite safe in saying-I hope I am-that the Minister of Veterans Affairs does not countenance and will not allow such a threat to be made to silence the veteran who might criticize the type of house he was getting. I think it was most unbecoming any man to make a threat of that kind. Mr. Murchison went on to say:
We have fortunately only a few samples of criticism of the type I referred to. Some of it developed in Calgary.
He was referring to statements made by me in the house in regard to the Calgary development. He went on:
I am glad that Mr. Harkness is here because it is in his constituency. It was not Mr. Harkness that spearheaded this criticism of what has been done there. . . .
I want to exonerate the hon. member for Calgary East from any criticism that I have made in the house in this regard. I take full responsibility for any statement that I have made. It was not in my constituency, and therefore I have nothing to gain by it personally. I have no votes to solicit. I have no other motive than to see that these veterans are given that which is their due. Mr. Murchison endeavoured to place on the record a statement. He said:
We have voluntary statements from some of the veterans concerned such as this. . . .
Then he went on to read a statement, but he did not give the name of the person. I think that was not intentional because he readily sent me a copy when I telephoned him for it. I will read the copy. The only difference is in the salutation and the complimentary close. It is dated March 30, 1946, and the address is 605-25th Ave. N.E., Calgary, Alberta. This is how it starts:
To whom it may concern-
May I suggest that that reads more like a circular than a personal letter.
To whom it may concern:
Having read the report in the Herald, March 29, in which Mr. Johnston says that our homes are falling apart, I would like to state that no such condition exists in my home. I am quite satisfied with the construction of my home throughout.	,
When looking for a home last fall I examined quite a few houses in various stages of construction, also some completed homes. In my estimation, the V.L.A. houses were a good deal better than any I had seen.
In these houses there are a few slight mistakes which are being rectified-
Notice the contradiction.
-and when they are properly finished I am quite sure I will have a home comparable to any in the city.
Previous to the war I was employed by the A. B. Cushing Company, of this city, and while there I served my apprenticeship as a carpenter.
Yours truly,
(Signed) D. Downie.
Having read that, I want to refer you, Mr. Chairman, to a letter that I received from the veterans committee which was sent to me by the chairman. It is dated April 4. This was after I had made my statement in the house to which the Minister of Veterans Affairs took great exception. The letter reads:
C. E. Johnston,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Johnston:
On Wednesday evening, April 3, 1946, a meeting of the veterans' group of Tuxedo Park small holdings, was held in the home of Mr. Don Sutherland. We wish to extend our sincere thanks to you for your efforts on our behalf.
There were 16 veterans present and it was unanimously decided to notify you of our complete and entire agreement with your remarks as quoted in Hansard.
I pause here to say that I intend to read to this committee the names of the persons who were present at that meeting where the decision was unanimous. The letter goes on:
We firmly believe-
That is, all the veterans present.
-that a first-class finish could have been made in the first place as cheaply or cheaper than w'as done plus cost of repairs.
The repairs promised us by V.L.A. have now been started, and V.L.A. promised-
They were mostly promises.
-these repairs will be finished to our entire satisfaction. There are quite a number of trivial inspections-
Note that.
-taking place at the moment but these inspections are all carried on during day time. It is suggested by the group that an inspection be carried on during the evening when the men are home. We can then show that our complaints are justified.
Supply-Veterans Affairs

I would have thought that when an inspector went around to investigate these complaints he would make his inspection when the man of the house was at home. But definitely the inspectors did not want to find him home and they did not go to make their inspections at the time the veteran would be home. The letter goes on:
The V.L.A. has approached several owners.
These were the voluntary statements to which Mr. Murchison referred and addressed, " To whom it may concern."

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What was the date of that letter? ..

April 4. It goes on:
The Y.L.A. has apprpached several owners, seven in number, within the last few days. They requested letters'

This was not a case of letters being written voluntarily.	.
-be written concerning our feelings about the homes, and the progress being made in the rectification of the previously lodged complaints. These letters in reply-
Note this. These letters, "in reply" were by veterans who were present at that meeting.
These letters, "in reply", stated

I draw particular attention to this:
-complete accordance with your statements and also the progress being made by V.L.A. in repairing the houses.
That bears out everything I have said. But so far we have not had produced those letters which were solicited by the Y.L.A. It goes on:
They also stated satisfaction will ultimately come about in most cases when these repairs have been made. This, however, does not make restitution to those of us who have had to spend considerable money personally to repair poor workmanship.
Kindest regards from all of us and again assuring you of our complete cooperation.
Yours,
H. S. Moore, (committee member).
P.S. Attached is list of veterans who attended meeting.
Then follows a list of the names, and the man's name is here whose letter was put on the report of the committee. He fully accepts my statements made in the house. The names are:
C. G-. Ingram, 448 25th avenue N.E.
C.	Jesson, 441 27th avenue N.E.
W. A. Dich, 445 27th avenue N.E.
R. T. Carlson, 606 25th avenue N.E.
E. Snyden, 443 25th avenue N.E.
R. J. Arkley, 447 25th avenue N.E.
D.	Murdoch, 630 25th avenue N.E.
E.	S. Dunn, 626 25tli avenue N.E.
G. M. Huget. 425 27th avenue N.E.
D.	Downie, 605 25th avenue N.E.

That is the man who signed the letter quoted by Mr. Murchison. I am referring particularly to his name, because in the next list of names which I intend to read his name is missing:
D. Sutherland, 444 25th avenue N.E.
H. S. Moore, 416 25th avenue N.E.
R. Derbyshire. 539 25th avenue N.E.
D.	Moss 535 25th avenue N.E.
E.	K. Elton, 419 27th avenue N.E.
D. Dahl, 602 25th avenue N.E.
In most of these cases, Mr. Chairman, where some are, as I say, fairly satisfied, they have spent considerable money out of their own pockets to make adjustments in these houses which, as indicated in the letter, should have been done by the contractors in the first place.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I want to read to you the next submission which was made to the committee by Mr. Murchison; that is on page 770. He says:
Here is a statement by a responsible member of our advisory committee in Calgary.
Again, Mr. Murchison does not give the name of the person, and I do not think that was done intentionally, either, because he readily sent me the copy of the letter when I asked him for it. This was the letter; I will read from the copy which I have received, dated at 507 Grain Exchange building, Calgary, Alberta, March 30, 1946-incidentally, they were both written the same day-addressed to Mr. A. Findlater, regional supervisor, Veterans' Land Act, Calgary, Alberta, It states:
[DOT]-re houses built for veterans under Veterans' Land Act in Tuxedo Park, Calgary.
On the afternoon of March 29 I inspected a number of houses that had been sold to veterans, and also interviewed a number of the occupants. Every one of the houses I examined-
Notice that-"every one".
-I found have been substantially built, i.e., basement walls-
I want you to notice this particularly:

are quite sufficient to carry the houses erected thereon, and the sills and joists are well put in; heavy enough that there is no danger of the building sagging. In some cases-
It is marvellous how some people can make an emphatic statement and then contradict it in the next few lines.
In some cases the material used in the construction is not all No. 1 and apparently had not been properly seasoned.
Did I not make that statement? And did anybody before the committee ever contradict it? No, certainly not. And here this man confirms it.
As a result in some places it has shrunk, but not to any alarming extent. In view of the scarcity of material I consider that these dwellings have been as well constructed as could be reasonably expected. The workmanship in all cases-

Supply-Veterans Affairs
Notice this:
-could not be considered as first class.
That is what I emphasized when I was speaking here. The work was far from being first-class workmanship, and the results are showing up now.
But owing to the scarcity of skilled tradesmen, I believe it would be practically impossible to have a dwelling built within a reasonable time that would not show some slight defects such as casings around the doors and windows not being properly fitted.
"Slight defects!" Can you tell me it is a slight defect when the rain will blow right through the doors and windows?
Terrible!

He goes on:
The occupants whom I interviewed are well satisfied with their homes and while mentioning some slight defects here and there in the workmanship, stated that they are causing them no inconvenience but suggesting in some cases that a little later, when material and skilled tradesmen can be secured to better advantage than at present, some slight adjustments could be made.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: What is the matter with that?

The hon. member ought to come and live in these houses and find out. The writer goes on:
After inspecting the properties and interviewing the occupants I consider that there is absolutely no foundation for the reports that these houses were badly constructed and the occupants very much dissatisfied.
Yours truly,
W. D. Mackay,
Member of the regional advisory committee.
Below he says:
I hereby certify that the above is a true and exact copy of Mr. W. D. Mackay's letter dated 30th March, 1946.
(sgd) A. Findlater,
Regional Supervisor, Veterans' Land Act, Calgary, Alberta.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am going to leave it at that for the moment, other than to say that this report is so contradictory that nobody could intelligently expect any committee to believe such a statement as that. The writer says, first, that the houses are substantially built. I have pointed out to this committee that in some cases the joists do not even meet over the beam, and any man who calls himself an inspector and would say that that was satisfactorily built does not know much about the matter. Anybody who says that a house is satisfactorily built when the floors are sagging does not know much about his business. Anybody who says that a basement wall is properly built when the water comes right through the wall doesn't know much about what he is saying.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You are "off the beam", anyhow.

I may be off the beam; but the minister, like this house, is a little warped; and also the remark has been made that the water is getting in the man's basement. I have already referred to this. Incidentally, the minister, speaking on this matter in the house on July 22, said, Hansard, page 3715:
I want to say that I have abundant evidence-
That is a pretty strong expression, and I suppose the minister would not have used it unless he had.
-from the settlers themselves of their complete satisfaction with these houses.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Hear, hear.

The minister went on:
I have an official letter-
This ought to be worth something.
-from the city engineer of Calgary justifying these houses. This evidence disproves in their entirety the remarks made by the hon. member for Bow River.
I then said:
This was never disproved in the committee.
I shall be only too pleased to have this discussed and I hope the minister brings his evidence before the committee.
I want to hear that evidence and see whether he can disprove what I have said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It seems to me that the [DOT] hon. member has taken a great deal of time-
Forty minutes.
I am going to take some more, too.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
-to deal with something which, after all, is not nearly as serious as he would make out. On March 28 last, he made his speech in the house. The facts in regard to this matter are really very simple. On account of the housing shortage the officials under the Veterans Land Act permitted a number of veterans to move into some of these houses in Calgary before they were finished and before they were taken over from the contractors, in order to accommodate these veterans. The contractors had not completed their work; the final inspections had not taken place, and the contractors had not been paid in full and have not yet been paid. The settlers moved in in December and January. They drew attention to these defects. As I said, no final inspection has yet been made; there is no suggestion that the houses have been finally taken over, and no suggestion that

Supply-Veterans Affairs

they were in a shape to be finally taken over by the veterans; the veterans were just given shelter during the winter.
Exactly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend, I suppose, could say that these veterans should be kept on the street until the houses could be finished to the last nail. I wonder if that is what he means. The veiy kind of attack which the hon. member is making is rendering it difficult for our department to get contractors anywhere to be willing to turn over houses until they are finished to the last degree.
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I am saying, what is a fact, that the uproar which the hon. member has made on account of the houses that were turned over for temporary use of the veterans before they are finished has made other contractors, who are jealous of their reputation, and afraid of being similarly attacked, fearful of turning over houses until they are absolutely finished. That is what the hon. gentleman has accomplished, and that is not imagination; it is fact.
Now to proceed. I do not know whether Mr. Cawthorne, who wrote the following letter, is another member of the advisory committee, but I take it the hon. member is making out that this gentleman in Calgary did not know what he was talking about, that the government made Mr. Cawthorne sign anything he [DOT] was asked to sign, and that my hon. friend is the only one who can give evidence before the house which can be relied on. It is a most amazing reflection for him to make on his fellow citizens of Alberta. I am sure they will be pleased to -hear it. However, this is what Mr. Cawthorne said:
All adjustments needed are of a very minor nature-
And remember, these are houses not yet finished, not yet turned over.
Who wrote that letter?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Cawthorne, justice of the peace. I suppose he is appointed by your government.
All adjustments needed are of a very minor nature and no difficulty is anticipated in having them attended to. These homes are outstanding in external appearance and will certainly be a credit to the community and the veterans who will own them.
The sweeping assertions made by the hon. member are certainly unjustified . . .
I hope the hon. member does not report that gentleman to the premier of Alberta for saying that.
I think I will.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: We would not do that and I do not think you should.
On a point of order-
Order.
I have no objection-
Take your medicine.
He can't take it.
I have no objection to the minister reading an official report from an engineer-
He is not minister yet.

-but I want it distinctly understood that when I asked to have reports tabled it was refused me on the ground that they were official. If he reads the reports I demand that the other reports I asked for be tabled.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You will get the whole lot of them.
Why did you not give them before?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Because I was debarred by the mles of the house. You will get more than you want.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: This is a report from the city engineer.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You will be sorry you ever started it.
Oh no, I won't.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
This is from the city engineer of Calgary. I suppose the hon. gentleman knows he is reliable. I hope he would not suggest that this gentleman would write something that was incorrect. He says:
The houses appear to be structurally sound, and from the appearance-
Does my hon. friend suggest that the city engineer of Calgary cannot be relied upon and that only the hon. member, with his superman, X-ray vision can see something that nobody else can see? I knew the hon. member attributed to himself powers and visions that no one else had, but I do not think he would suggest that he can see things which ordinary mortals cannot see. This is what the engineer says:
The houses appear to be structurally sound and from the appearance of the finish the class of workmanship has been average. It is needless to mention that with the difficulty in obtaining material, and with having to use green lumber in some instances, that refitting of doors and windows is unavoidable, that shrinkage of floors cannot be prevented. It appears, however, that where such conditions have existed

Supply-Veterans Affairs
that they have been remedied, that provision has
been made to relay new floors, tighten windows, doors, et cetera, in any found requiring this work . . .
The prices that the houses are being erected for are well within present-day building costs. In fact, I doubt if any private individual could obtain a price on a similar house for a figure within $500 of the costs that these are being erected for. On the whole, these are attractive looking houses, and very -well equipped.
What is the cost?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
That is in the record which I have already tabled. He says:
On the whole, these are attractive looking houses and very well equipped.
I have no great objection to that report.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I would think not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That is the opinion of the city engineer of Calgary, not an official of our department, not a man who would make a statement like that unless he knew it to be correct.
He confirms everything I have said.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Do not interrupt; keep your seat.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
In regard to this contract in Calgary, the contract for these houses was let after public advertisement and competitive tenders, to the lowest bidder, Bennett and White Limited, one of the outstanding construction firms in western Canada. The contract has been administered under supervision of the district construction supervisor appointed by the civil service commission. The construction supervisor in turn supervises the local engineers and inspectors in charge of day-to-day operations, also appointed by the civil service commission.
The houses were built under the trying conditions that confront everyone trying to build in the west. Of course, certain difficulties did appear from time to time and the government is holding the contractor responsible for making them good, and has always done so. The contractor has not been settled with, and will not be settled with until the houses pass inspection and come up to specifications.
In regard to these houses, twenty-two are now finished and occupied; eight are not completely finished yet but are occupied; eight will be ready for occupancy in a week, and twenty-two are ready for flooring and painting, and furnace work is proceeding. We are advised by the chief of the building and supplies division of veterans affairs department that the district construction supervisor reports on 63260-307J
August 14 that all items of work that needed repairs and adjustments, as reported from last February, have now been taken care of, except that in certain houses sufficient fir flooring had not been delivered to replace softwood floors in upstairs rooms. The shortage of fir flooring in western Canada is acute and, according to>
the timber control regulations, they were not supposed to lay hardwood floors in the upstairs. But owing to poor quality of softwood flooring supplied through the timber control office last fall, an exception was made in the case of Calgary.
I would say to the hon. member that I do not suppose he intended this result to happen. I suppose he was called in and it was not explained to him that the houses were not finished, were not supposed to be finished, were not turned over, were not in any way accepted by the government, but the veterans were permitted to move into them before they were finished in order that they might have shelter. I suppose the hon. gentleman acted in good faith; but I say to him in all sincerity that we have had great difficulty in getting contractors throughout Canada, who are jealous of their good reputations, to permit us to have houses occupied by veterans, though it would provide them with shelter, until those houses are finished right up to the last item of the specification; and the effect of the hon. gentleman's charge has been that veterans who could have obtained shelter have been denied it on account of the charges made against this firm of contractors.
As I say, I do not suppose the hon. gentleman intended this result, but the only effect has been what I have stated. The houses have been finished in accordance with the specifications, as they would have been in any event. He does not need to think that anything he has said has contributed to these houses being brought up to specification, because before the contractors would have been paid and the houses accepted they would have had to pass-the final inspection of the government under which all defects would have been corrected. So that the only result of what the hon. gentleman said has been the one I have mentioned. I consider it most unfortunate that he should have made his charge against contractors who did not take the position they might have taken and refuse to turn over these houses until they were absolutely finished. Their only reward has been this attack by the hon. member, and to have their names besmirched from one end of Canada to the other. That: is a very poor reward for those people who* departed from the letter of the contract which they made with the government in order to
Supply-Veterans Affairs

provide shelter- for veterans. As I say, I do not think he intended it in that way, but it is unfortunate.

I think the parliamentary
assistant has made out a very weak case for himself.
You are the only one who thinks so.

Oh, am I? The report of the engineer confirmed everything I said; it does not contain one thing to prove that what I said was wrong. This talk about the reputation of the contractors being at stake is just so much eyewash, because when the people moved into those houses there was nothing left unfinished about them that the contractor could not complete without any inconvenience to those who had moved in. That is the most common thing you ever heard of. I'll bet you there is not one house into which people move to-day with everything absolutely completed before the family moves in. It just isn't done. When they say they cannot build houses under the conditions under which they built these houses without having these defects, I say anyone who makes that statement does not know anything about building. I built a house at the very same time these houses were going up, and I would defy anyone to come and find the rain running into my house, or water running through my basement wall, or the floors shrinking; and I had the same material available to me that was available to them. The only difference was that in every case the government had a priority. They talk now about the floors shrinking. Well, why would the government put spruce flooring into a place, anyway, when it was all green? We are told they could not get fir flooring. Well, I got it, and everybody else around got it. Why could the government not get it? That is just silliness; and if my hon. friend thinks anybody is going to take that into consideration he is wrong.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I imagine all these people must be dishonest-according to the hon. gentleman.

I agree almost entirely with the engineer's report. I have no criticism of him, because he pointed out quite clearly where the defects were. The parliamentary assistant suggested that the contractors must make good. He must understand that some of these veterans have already spent well over $200 to fix up a house that was new, a house that had been built according to plans and specifications. You cannot tell me that a house has been built according to plans and specifica-

tions and has the defects I have mentioned. Certainly not. Let us see how they lived up to their specifications. Let me read another letter to you, Mr. Chairman. I want you to remember that, according to the parliamentary assistant, the charge I made was unjustified; that I have done a great injustice to these contractors; that otherwise these veterans would not have had these houses. I say to you, sir, that we might better have built one good house and had one veteran well satisfied than build two poor houses and have two veterans dissatisfied. The parliamentary assistant says these people are out of the storm. I do not think they are. The storm goes right through the walls, right through the windows, right through the basement. They might just as well be outside. That is no excuse.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Remember that what you say is being taken down by Hansard and will be read all over the place.

That is an extremely poor argument for the government to put up. The minister says I want to put this on Hansard. Why did they not take action at first, when these veterans went after them, when they tried by every means at their disposal to get the authorities in Calgary to do something? It was expressly understood at that'first meeting, that nothing would be done except through the proper channels; and I so advised them.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We took action long before you made your flamboyant speech.
With your trivial inspections, but they did not take place until afterwards.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is nonsense. You do not know what you are talking about.
Do you believe that yourself?
Yes, I do.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Let us get on with the work of the house.

We shall get on with it, and we shall get on with the position of these veterans, too. Here is another letter sent to me by the committee, dated May 31:
It seems some time since we had the pleasure of communicating with you and the present time seems most appropriate, to give you a short resume of our activities here, and reparations to our houses since you last heard from us.
V.L.A. have had some repairs made-
This was after you started to fix up the places, to make the repairs.

Supply-Veterans Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Long before you were ever seen over there.

It goes on:
-including a little painting and new floors-
Was my charge wrong, when I complained about the floors? They had to go back and put in new floors; and then they said I was wrong.
-put in the upstairs of several two-storey homes. We all have outside water faucets now-
Quite a contribution!
-and a few basement traps have been repaired.
Was I wrong in the statement I made?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: We inspected all the houses, all over Canada.

The letter goes on:
However, there is no sign of sidewalks or eavestroughing and little if any hope of getting these at any date * apropos to our meeting this afternoon at V.L.A. with Mr. Wiber (inspector V.L.A., Edmonton).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? Would he suggest that we should not have allowed these veterans into these houses, unfinished as they were, until they were finished? Would he rather have had them kept out? Did we do right in letting them into the shelter of these houses before they were finished, or should we have kept them out until these houses were all completed?
Now, now; surely you do not mean a statement like that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Answer the question.
If that is the answer to my charges I think it is very poor.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Admittedly these houses were not finished, and I am asking: should we have let them be occupied before they were finished, or should we have made the people wait until the houses were completed?

Answer the
question.
Certainly I shall answer it. Keep still over there, and I will tell you.

been tarred there is something definitely wrong. That is clear when men had to be sent out there to break the wTall with electric hammers in order to repair it. As I said when I made my last statement to the house, I estimated that it would cost between $500 and $1,000 to repair these houses. This estimate has been proven correct, and if this House of Commons allows these conditions to prevail and allows twenty-three or twenty-four veterans who are buying these houses to be treated in this way, I say it is a crime to treat in this way veterans who have been overseas. They are entitled to every consideration. The veteran who has fought for this country has every right to fair treatment, just the same as anybody else, and that is all I am asking. I am not looking for glory myself. I do not care if a word of mine on this subject is ever published. But I want these veterans to get a square deal.

speechtext: I shall be very glad to take the matter up with the chief priority officer at once.

I should' like to mention a case which proves that the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs and the pension board are honest and sincere in their service. When I have placed before them the facts of needy cases, in not one instance have they failed. I will give one example. A farmer about a hundred miles west of Fort William said to me one day, "I hope you treat my boy better than I was treated." I said, "What is the matter with you? You look honest and you look healthy." "Well," he said, "I have not been able to do a decent day's work since I was discharged." And I believed him. I placed the case before the pension board. He was then getting $9 a month pension. Then he was sent to Deer Lodge hospital, near Winnipeg, and was given treatment for nearly a year. They found they could not treat him successfully and they gave him a pension of $60 a month. I think it is only due to our officials that I and those like me who have seen cases of this kind get honest and generous treatment should publicly mention the fact.

I should like to refer to'a question asked two or three days ago by the hon. member for Vancouver South, and also mentioned to-night by the hon. member for Fraser Valley, concerning small holdings. I was a member of the veterans committee. Most of us thought our job was done when the committee was finished, but a new interpretation of "small holdings" has been brought in, not by the Veterans' Land Act branch or the Department of Veterans Affairs, nor by the veterans affairs committee, but by the Minister of Reconstruc-

tion, and so I think any member of the veterans affairs committee should be quite free to discuss the matter here in the House of Commons.
The first mention of small holdings as far as the soldier is concerned came with this little pamphlet published by the Hon. Ian A. Mackenzie, Minister of Veterans Affairs, sent to all soldiers overseas in 1942. On page 4, in outlining what was to be done for the soldiers when they returned, it is stated in paragraph (b) that "small holding settlements means an urban, semi-rural or rural home of limited acreage located"-this phrase is especially important

"close to an employment opportunity." Then there follow almost two pages of explanation of this, and then one significant thing: "It is important that small holdings settlements referred to in (b) above should not be thought of only"-let me repeat -"only in relation to the larger and more highly industrialized centres of Canada." The rest of the page explains how the veteran who does not want to be a farmer is to be given this added security, if he has industrial employment, of having a home, a victory garden and a bit of land outside high-taxed areas in the city. Then further, in 1944, 1945 and 1946 all of us overseas received these "Back to Civil Life" pamphlets, which explained it still further; and since the war has been over the Veterans' Land Act administration have gone ahead-I think very well- in my own riding, in settling soldiers into these small holdings of an acre, or of half an acre in the vicinity of industrial employment. Now, in speaking of districts in my riding, I do not want to be parochial in my outlook, but fortunately the hon. member for Vancouver South three or four days ago mentioned in the house that, in the Vancouver area, certainly the most suitable places for small holdings were North Vancouver and Burnaby, both in my riding. The hon. member for Fraser Valley said the same thing this evening; and the minister, who is the member for Vancouver Centre, must certainly recognize that the two working-man districts of the Vancouver area are North Vancouver and Burnaby, both with ample land suitable for this purpose. This recent regulation of the Minister of Reconstruction, which was not discussed or approved by the veterans affairs committee, now limits these small holdings to communities of less than five thousand or more than fifteen miles from a metropolitan area, which, to my mind, just throws out of the window the small holdings which were promised to the veteran. A young man having industrial employment in Vancouver formerly

Supply-Veterans Affairs
could take up a small holding in North Vancouver, Coquitlam, Burnaby or where he would have the advantage of low tax and have a victory garden, the suburbs of the town, so that industrial employment would be available to him. But that has been destroyed, not by the Department of Veterans Affairs, but by the Department of Reconstruction in connection with its new housing scheme. This is the proper place for the minister to give me a satisfactory answer, and it will not do for him simply to say, as has been said to the hon. member for Vancouver South and the hon. member for Fraser Valley, that the matter is under consideration. He should tell us why the department is throwing out of the window these promises made to the veterans that those with industrial jobs would have small holdings in adjacent suburbs made available to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver North. I wonder if all the members of the committee are familiar with the evolution of the Veterans Land Act. I wrote to the Prime Minister on October 30, 1939, asking for the formation of a committee on demobilization and reestablishment and that was acceded to on November 2, 1939, when the war was very young. We had a committee formed under General McDonald, who has now been called away from us, and the organizing genius of that committee was my deputy minister, Walter Woods. We formed fourteen subcommittees. One subcommittee was to deal with land settlement. We got what we believed were the finest experts from the various departments and called in practical farmers from all across Canada in every provence to advise us, and they devoted eighteen months of study to the subject before making their recommendation. One from Winnipeg was killed in an aeroplane accident at Armstrong, Mr. Grier, just after he had attended one of our meetings.
Although I was not administering soldier settlement at that time, I asked for a parliamentary committee in 1942 to which would be appointed some of our veteran members, mostly farmer veteran members of the house. That committee went carefully into the report, with the guidance of and in consultation with the present director, and we drew up a bill. Although I was not the minister, I made a suggestion that that committee form a department of veterans affairs in Canada, and the committee agreed to that proposal and sent a report to the house, which this house accepted in 1942.
What I am coming to is basically fundamental. The main idea the committee had
in mind at that time was that the Veterans' Land Act should be for the settlement of farms for veterans, while the other features were incidental. The small holdings and commercial fishermen's features were incidental. Perhaps unfortunately, however, these two features became the most popular parts of the legislation and, especially in view of housing conditions in Canada, there arose a tremendous outcry for small holdings and housing, because the terms were very favourable.
At that time, as the committee knows, there were three agencies in connection with housing: finance, wartime housing, and ourselves, the Veterans Land Act, in a small way. We built 2,700 houses last year. Our terms were so much more favourable that a great demand was made that we should go into urban housing. We felt, however, that if we did we were destroying the fundamental principles of the Veterans Land Act because our main purpose is settlement and not housing.
I greatly appreciate the strength of the presentation made by my hon. friend in regard to certain areas with which I am familiar, and I will discuss the matter with my colleague.
* As a matter of fact, it is being discussed now, and I shall do all I can to present the ideas that my hon. friend has expressed.	[DOT]

I
appreciate the minister's remarks, but he has not answered my question. All he has done is to say that a most careful study was given the subject by himself to begin with; then a committee of experts was appointed, and then the 1942 parliamentary committee on veterans affairs and that then they turned out this booklet which they sent to the troops, from which I will quote the main purpose in view:
Thus the veterans land act is the flexible measure under which

And this is in black face type: not one and subsidiary objectives, but "four main types of establishment are available." The first is farming, and, second, there is the small holding. What I as a veteran, and! a member of the veterans affairs committee, object to strongly is that the minister, having shown this foresight in 1939, the department and its experts having done such a good jo'b in establishing: provisions for small holdings, the veterans affairs committee of 1942 having threshed the matter out and approved these provisions, and the department having presented these promises to the soldiers in booklet form, the soldiers having believed in it, and soldiers-returning over a period of one or two years having been able to take advantage of it, it is then closed off The minister gives no reason: why it was closed off. He simply says, "We are not going into urban settlement". But
Supply-Veterans Affairs

these are not urban districts. Take the almost rural districts of Deep Cove and Lynn Valley, in North Vancouver, where veterans with industrial jobs in Vancouver could live. Will the minister tell the veterans, will he tell the members of this house, why the veterans affairs committee has changed from the policy of allowing soldiers with industrial jobs to get into these districts, not too remote from the city, where there is low taxation and where they can operate a small holding? Why this great departure? The minister should say why the change has been made, not by his department but by the Department of Reconstruction. If he will tell us that, then we shall be able to tell the veterans the reason for the change. But for the minister to tell me in his pleasant manner that the matter is under consideration is not good enough New matters are considered, but changes should be explained. Why was the change made? As a Vancouver member I should like to know just where veterans with small industrial jobs in Vancouver are to settle, if not in North Vancouver and Burnaby.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: All I can say is that I will bring my hon. friend's very able presentation to the attention of my colleague.

I am like my friend the hon. member for Bow River. All I want is an answer. We had a certain policy and it has now been changed1. It is not a new matter to be studied and considered. It is something which should be explained to [DOT]every veteran member of the house, why the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply and the Central Mortgage Corporation changed the promises made officially to the veterans and the policy under which such an excellent job had been done. I was glad the minister went into detail to tell us how much consideration had been given over a period of years to the setting up of these four main objectives, though one month ago the provisions for small holdings near cities was thrown out of the window.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It was not thrown out of the window. I want to be as emphatic as my hon. friend if he wants to be emphatic.
I do.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
It is not a change of policy but a development of policy, the result of the coordination of three departments under
the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply_
that is, the department of his own, the Department of Finance and the Department of Veterans Affairs in so far as houses are concerned -leaving complete independence to the Department of Veterans Affairs in its own

affairs. I am taking most sympathetic note of my hon. friend's presentation, and I shall discuss it with the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply at the earliest possible moment.

May I ask the minister just where veterans working in his own city riding of Vancouver Centre will qualify for small holdings close enough so that they will not bankrupt themselves by transportation back and forth? What districts can they settle in since North Vancouver and Burnaby are not available to them?
iMr. MACKENZIE: I am sympathetic to my hon. friend's remarks. Take Burnaby, which he represents in part. The taxation rate there is tremendously high in certain parts in connection with soldier settlement.

The minister knows that the district of Burnaby has given to veterans with small holdings a special concession of taxes at $60 an acre, and the district of North Vancouver has also given special concession, the rate set by his department and now the veterans are rewarded by the department throwing this out of the window. I insist on that phrase. It has been thrown out of the window.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I object to that. I have not thrown anything out of the window.

Then I shall merely say that this combination of the Department of Reconstruction, the Department of Finance and the Department of Veterans Affairs have flung it out the window, and I am very sorry to see that the Department of Veterans Affairs had any part of that.
I should like to ask the minister who decides what regions are or are not applicable, as to employment opportunity?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The Minister of Reconstruction, after consultation with those who would represent the specific regions.
Then will there be made available a list of those regions which would be suitable for small holdings?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I see no reason why not.
Is there such a list?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
We have had drawn up under the director, who is present here to-night, a list of regions throughout Canada as far as our programme goes, which is rather modest. We have been asked to build 4,000 units this year out of a total of 80,000 units throughout Canada as between private enterprise and governmental agencies. For four or five years now the director has been select-

Supply-Veterans Affairs
ing areas for small holdings. Unfortunately, or at least I think unfortunately, it has developed into group settlement on a fairly large scale; that is, with houses in great units. My own idea would have been-probably I do not know very much about it-individual settlements and holdings out five, six, eight or ten miles, for those who would have employment opportunities in the cities; but they have developed into groups of settlements adjacent to urban boundaries.

In view of the minister's answer, then, I hope a list of the areas which are considered suitable for such small h'oldings will be made available to veterans so that they may know what they are doing.
May I take up another matter arising out of my own experience in connection with the efforts of soldiers to get into some of these particular units? I understand that the department now requires them to present the certificate of an employer, stating that the particular veteran is now in permanent employment. What are the regulations in that regard? It seems to me there is too much opportunity here for throwing out the applications, and the boys are feeling considerable resentment about it. A number of boys in a certain area of my constituency are anxious to get settled on small holdings. They make their application. Finally, after a good deal of correspondence some representative goes to them, and the boys now find that one of the requirements is that their employer sign a statement for the department that the particular applicant is now in permanent employment. Is that one of the requirements?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Certainly; that was the basic purpose of the act, and unanimously endorsed by the committee in 1942, that small holdings were ancillary to industrial employment, and would not necessarily be selfsustaining, as against the settlement of farm areas which would be entirely farming settlements.
But do you require as one of the requisites, in the case of a man wanting to get on a small holding-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Not in all cases, but it is done in some cases.
That is the very point. Why the discrimination; and in which regions do you require such a statement from the employer?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We require a reasonable anticipation of success on the settlement.
That is agreed, but there must be certain areas-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No; it is not regional at all. It is personal, in regard to certam industrial employment areas.

Then can we say that in a certain small city in the west you would require that the employer sign a statement that the particular veteran making application for a small holding has employment, and that no veteran will have his application accepted unless he can produce such a statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is no complete prohibition anywhere, but we endeavour to ascertain whether there is probable employment in view, and that is for the protection of the settler himself.
From there where does it go? Who has the final decision? Take an actual case of a man-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The local advisory
committee, of which there is one in almost every community in Canada.
The advisory committee of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.
What committee is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The number on the committee is not definitely stated; there may be three or five or seven. I am told there are now forty-five of these committees in Canada.
You mean that every area in Canada is covered by some advisory committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
And the applicant has to satisfy that committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is it.
This particular item covers the administration of soldier settlement. Does this have to do with the old soldier settlement administration?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

Could the minister give us the figures for the last two years, separately, as to the cost of administration of soldier settlement, as nearly as they have it; the number of soldier settlers who have been deprived of their holdings, that is the settlers of world war No. 1, and also whether or not those holdings have been resold?
